sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive failure mode reported is the old sign-them-up-and-sort-them-out model. Mohr Marketing says the special masters and the court have moved into strict docket control, essentially Lone Pine standards, where every new Bard filing needs immediate proof of use and specific injury evidence, and firms still running the old playbook are burning capital on cases that will be dismissed with prejudice before they ever see a settlement tier [agO8HeUx95E @ 00:00:40]. The proof problem is mechanical. Lawsuit Tracker warns that medical records usually get purged every 7 to 10 years, that the mesh brand lives in the surgical report from the original implant, and that the revision report is what documents the perforation or other injury [orLyLTC8fiA @ 00:01:52]. On PowerPort, Jennifer Elwell of Berger Montague says evaluation requires close record review for product ID, diagnosis, removal and replacement-device information, plus the implant-to-injury timeline, and flags limitations exposure because most states run two to three years unless the discovery rule can extend it [flwkUvC50CU @ 00:15:16]. On the CPAP matrix, Fantini's list starts with the serial number sticker as proof of usage, then proof of the qualifying compensable injury, then the enhancement-category records [voWGMGOyvtQ @ 00:04:01]. Every trap on this list is a missing document rather than a weak liability theory.

Signed settlements create their own trap. Kelsey Stokes says litigation alone can run two years if you are lucky up to seven or eight, and once a deal is inked, administration of a claimant pool the size of Bard's can take two to three more, with clients angry that they have a deal and no check even while counsel hits every deadline [IPkB5-wL-oY @ 00:04:37]. Co-administering counsel David Hobbs reports spending 20 to 30 to 50 percent of a day answering case-counsel questions about what to submit and how, plus running training so reviewers judge the covered injuries correctly [IPkB5-wL-oY @ 00:03:31]. King Law delivers the same message from the firm side: this is not a car-accident case where the check arrives two weeks after the release, and administering the Bard money will take well over a year on its own [Is4DHXZ5JIM @ 00:02:12]. The reversal story is Medtronic. O'Brien says Covidien kept plaintiffs on a tolling agreement, told them not to file while a global deal was explored, then changed general counsel and pulled the agreement entirely, which is why the Covidien MDL trails the dockets that already settled [JlBWnsNpbyc @ 00:10:30]. A defendant's settlement posture is revocable, and inventory parked under a tolling deal can be forced back into full litigation overnight.

The economics checks are blunt. On NEC, Fantini runs the Abbott inventory math: three firms, a $675 million deal that included the $495 million Gill verdict, which Fantini reads as roughly another $175 million for about 2,000 cases, or around $80,000 a case, with specific causation fights and premature-baby plaintiffs, concluding it is not the most recommended tort unless you want to get a little risky before the window closes [2lQbSEVsxgE @ 00:03:50]. Host Mark Ryu presses harder: these cases have historically been expensive to acquire, attrition hits once the medical records come out, and at $80,000 a piece buying them may not make sense against the fee, though one that crosses your desk still has value [2lQbSEVsxgE @ 00:04:28]. Verdict risk cuts both ways. The first Bard PowerPort bellwether ended in a partial defense verdict and a partially deadlocked jury, and even the $40 million Divelbliss win came without a fraudulent-concealment finding or punitive damages [t8pdtQfiTLM @ 00:03:02]. On Bard hernia mesh, Fantini reported the judge canceling the fourth bellwether, ordering mediation, and setting a May 24 report deadline with remands on the table if the parties stayed at an impasse [UP0ve0ms-ik @ 00:05:15]. Budget for hung juries, trimmed damages and judicial resets, not just headline awards.

callout.title: Four Hard Stops Before Funding Device Inventory
callout.body: Each stop below traces to a loss, reversal, or bottleneck practitioners reported on hernia mesh, PowerPort, and NEC dockets.
items: Reject any Bard hernia mesh file lacking immediate proof of use and specific injury evidence, because Lone Pine style docket control now dismisses padded inventory with prejudice [Mohr Marketing — agO8HeUx95E @ 00:00:40].
Secure the original implant surgical report naming the mesh product before records hit the typical 7-to-10-year purge window [Lawsuit Tracker — orLyLTC8fiA @ 00:01:52].

Never treat a defendant tolling agreement as a settled outcome; Medtronic pulled its agreement after a general counsel change and forced the Covidien MDL into litigation [Cut to the Chase Network — JlBWnsNpbyc @ 00:10:30].

Underwrite NEC acquisition against roughly $80,000 per case, expensive acquisition, and attrition once medical records surface before spending a dollar on leads [Jon and Marc — 2lQbSEVsxgE @ 00:04:28].

chapters.pull_quote: “Stop buying noise and start acquiring evidence.” — Mohr Marketing (agO8HeUx95E @ 00:02:54)
action_checklist: Collect the implant record, every revision surgery report, and all subsequent treatment records on each hernia mesh client to maximize value in the settlement process [Case Works — oc04hOYvUBA @ 00:01:41].

Disqualify pain-only callers at intake and route them to a nurture sequence, keeping acquisition spend on confirmed revisions with identifiable product lines [Mohr Marketing — agO8HeUx95E @ 00:02:05].

Sort Covidien files into buckets: resorbable-barrier ventral products, ProGrip inguinal products, and bare polyester mesh, because each carries a different injury theory [Jon and Marc — IPkB5-wL-oY @ 00:09:34].
On PowerPort intake, pull product ID, diagnosis, removal and replacement-device information from the medical records before signing [Case Works — flwkUvC50CU @ 00:14:53].

For matrix-driven device settlements, gather the serial number sticker as proof of usage, proof of the qualifying injury, and enhancement-category treatment records [Case Works — voWGMGOyvtQ @ 00:04:01].
Budget a case-specific expert report for every new Bard hernia mesh filing, since it must be filed soon after the lawsuit [Cut to the Chase Network — JlBWnsNpbyc @ 00:17:25].

chapters.question_prompt: What is happening in the toxic-exposure, consumer, and emerging tech dockets, and what do settlement rules mean for timing?
chapters.title: Toxic Exposure, Consumer & Emerging Dockets
chapters.subtitle: PFAS/AFFF water contamination and individual injury claims, Camp Lejeune, Roundup, paraquat, hair relaxer, Uber, social media addiction and Grok image cases, 95% participation thresholds, and year-end settlement watch
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners from Broughton Partners, King Law, Napoli Shkolnik and Tort Talk converge on one operating truth: toxic-exposure dockets pay only after defendants can count their liability, so filing deadlines, plaintiff fact sheets and deficiency rounds are the real gatekeepers. The AFFF MDL ballooned to 131,000 filings, was scrubbed toward 80,000 to 90,000, and resolved for about $7.35 billion covering 115,000 to 120,000 claims across six injuries, with Michael Stanisci forecasting first funds around the second half of 2028. Steve Smith pegs the Roundup class average near $70,000 and Depo-Provera at $150,000 to $200,000, and sells a $10,000-a-month Consortium that spreads capital across underwritten torts. Disagreements are sharp: Smith avoids MDLs for state-court premiums while Tort Talk works MDL enrollment mechanics, and Miller & Zois forecasts mid-six-figure AFFF payouts.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus: Countable Liability, Documented Claims, Trusted Jockeys
paragraphs: The baseline rule every toxic-exposure operator repeats is that defendants do not write checks until they can count the claimants on the docket. Steve Smith of Broughton Partners explains that the AFFF judge imposed a hard-cut filing deadline because 3M would not agree to a global number without knowing its liability, and the deadline showed exactly how many claimants it would have to pay [IHvCfh-WJ6E @ 00:04:23]. Smith's second appearance puts numbers on the shock: the market expected roughly 60,000 to 70,000 AFFF cases, 131,000 got filed, the judge was disgusted, and the first trial was postponed while the docket was scrubbed for dual representation, medical qualification and exposure location down to roughly 80,000 to 90,000 [-H3O5pPP-XA @ 00:07:28]. Robert King of King Law reads the same tape from the filing side: the fall 2025 bellwether was postponed indefinitely, Case Management Order 35 allowed mass filing against a deadline, and that told King the judge believed the parties could reach an agreement [aOm5hBG6t9s @ 00:00:38]. Joe Fantini on Tort Talk confirms the endpoint: a roughly $7.35 billion AFFF settlement resolving 115,000 to 120,000 personal injury claims across the top six injuries [08ES8nUZRYk @ 00:00:39]. The operating lesson is that inventory size and deadline discipline drive resolution timing more than trial rhetoric.

The second point of agreement is that a claim is only as strong as the paper behind it. Andrew Kroner of Napoli Shkolnik warns that courts in the MDL already require very specific proof for a case to remain viable, and that believing you were exposed or generally knowing you suffer from a PFAS-linked condition is not enough; clients need documented diagnoses and medical histories [S1VC15_WonY @ 00:01:44]. Kroner singles out ulcerative colitis, where symptoms can stretch across years and multiple providers, as a claim that needs pathology reports, diagnostic imaging, treatment histories and specialist evaluations [S1VC15_WonY @ 00:02:15]. Robert King frames the standard as two proofs: proof of injury, pulled through medical records the firm orders from various providers sometimes covering many years, and proof of exposure, meaning firefighter work history or residency inside a known contaminated water supply system [aOm5hBG6t9s @ 00:03:52]. On the consumer side, Salenger, Sack, Kimmel & Bavaro applies a parallel three-part screen to hair relaxer: years of use rather than once or twice, a documented brand that is part of the case, and a uterine, ovarian or endometrial cancer diagnosis sitting in the medical charts [ch5IVo6DOos @ 00:05:33]. Kroner expects courts to keep narrowing who qualifies because PFAS exposure is ubiquitous, so organized records preservation is the operator's insurance.

Third, practitioners agree that who litigates the inventory, and where it sits, changes the payout. Steve Smith tells referral firms the jockey matters as much as the horse, noting that Bayer settled with a handful of firms outside the Roundup class deal at a premium while class-only cases take lesser amounts [IHvCfh-WJ6E @ 00:02:55]. In NEC baby formula, Smith reports the MDL has had no trial success while state court cases have had great success, which is where the pressure comes in and why firm selection matters, because not all courts and venues are created equal [-H3O5pPP-XA @ 00:14:06]. Salenger, Sack, Kimmel & Bavaro describes bellwether trials as the mechanism that lets both sides see their strengths and weaknesses and promotes settlement across a docket of roughly 12,000 hair relaxer cases [ch5IVo6DOos @ 00:01:31]. Joe Fantini reads defense behavior the same way: after the October Uber bellwether settled in the MDL with about 4,600 cases still pending, Fantini concluded the days of Uber trials are done, and once defendants wave the flag on individual bellwethers, bigger settlements usually follow [ql3WYzhinZk @ 00:06:38]. Operators treat trial settlements, postponements and scheduling gaps as leading indicators for when to tighten inventory and prepare enrollment.

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers: Intake Screens, Enrollment Drills and Underwritten Buys
paragraphs: Intake screens are spelled out to the number. Elizabeth of Lawsuit Tracker lists the six filable AFFF injuries, namely kidney, liver, testicular and thyroid cancer, thyroid disease and ulcerative colitis, and qualifies claimants who were stationed on, lived on as a dependent, or worked on a military base, or who live where the utility water report shows over four parts per trillion of PFAS chemicals [tVouqZmWW5I @ 00:03:16]. Lawsuit Tracker's firm runs a 40-year latency window from exposure to diagnosis and openly tells claimants that other firms may set different criteria [tVouqZmWW5I @ 00:03:33]. Robert King's shop maps known contaminated systems by PWSID, the public water ID number, or by ZIP code, so residency can be matched to a contaminated supply [aOm5hBG6t9s @ 00:04:07]. For social media addiction, Joe Fantini gives the LexHive Podcast acquisition screen: a minor who started before age 16, used a platform for hours a week, and developed any mental health issue, from depression, anxiety and body issues up through school problems, abuse problems and suicidal thoughts [DQ8EXxoteKo @ 00:07:27]. Fantini sizes that market at maybe 200,000 to 250,000 eventual plaintiffs against under 10,000 cases pending today, which is why acquisition urgency has increased significantly.

Once a deal lands, the work becomes a deadline drill. In the AFFF settlement, Joe Fantini told firms to rush the full ID order into the portal by Friday, November 13, listing every case they believe belongs in the deal, followed by de-duping, proof of specific injuries and verification that water claimants lived at specific addresses during the relevant time periods [08ES8nUZRYk @ 00:01:19]. In talc, Fantini describes an uncapped $5.5 billion settlement with a 95% participation threshold across about 70,000 cancer cases, forcing firms to track down clients who moved or died and use the settlement mechanism to name a potential representative [NHmq2W3F_do @ 00:05:45]. Depo-Provera runs on an administrative docket Judge Rodgers created for roughly 6,000 settling cases, with November 30 as the deadline to move non-qualifying or opt-out cases onto the traditional docket under the Lone Pine fact sheet and expert report requirements [NHmq2W3F_do @ 00:07:41]. In the Missouri Roundup class, Fantini flags a 90-day opt-out window that requires a wet signature, not DocuSign, plus a copy of ID, so firms must review records, place each client on a tier, and counsel big-damages clients with recurrences or heavy chemo on whether to opt out [3Qxw8dtCCns @ 00:07:40].

The unit economics are explicit. Steve Smith positions Broughton Partners as a consultant rather than a lead vendor, with the Goldwater Law Firm handling advertising, intake and paid analytics so a referring firm takes on no new staff [IHvCfh-WJ6E @ 00:17:22]. The Consortium costs as little as $10,000 a month for one year, or $120,000, and pools each member with 24 other attorneys; every monthly one-hour Zoom spends 30 minutes on headlines and questions, then presents opportunities underwritten on cost per contract, attrition, expected value and timeline of settlement for a group vote, spreading the $120,000 across multiple torts and litigating firms with higher buying power [IHvCfh-WJ6E @ 00:18:21]. On case value, Smith expects Depo-Provera qualifying cases to average $150,000 to $200,000, backed by a greater than 5x increased risk against the 2x rule of thumb, with signing effectively closed by mid last year because most claimants were already retained [-H3O5pPP-XA @ 00:16:14]. Camp Lejeune shows the spread operators must price: Fantini reports the first bench trial asked for a little under $11 million, while the same case would have been about a $500,000 case had it settled through the EO [ql3WYzhinZk @ 00:04:06]. That gap is why the parties are fighting over a Lone Pine order versus a census of the 25 injuries.

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Venue is the sharpest split on the street. Steve Smith of Broughton Partners says the shop does everything to avoid MDLs, routing cases to partners who create their own traction, retain their own experts, and file in state court, because those firms keep landing higher claim values and are not blinded by common benefit fees that might push a firm to settle for lesser amounts [IHvCfh-WJ6E @ 00:15:28]. Smith uses NEC as the proof point: the MDL has had no trial success, while the cases held in state court have had great success, so not all courts and not all venues are created equal [-H3O5pPP-XA @ 00:14:06]. Smith still carves PFAS out as one of the rare dockets with no state court or individual firm play, calling it a global resolution [IHvCfh-WJ6E @ 00:03:39]. Joe Fantini of Tort Talk treats the state lane as a file-by-file call rather than a doctrine. In the Missouri Roundup class, Fantini tells firms to isolate the big files, such as a cancer recurrence or heavy chemo, and counsel those clients on opting out with a wet signature and ID inside the 90-day window, while weaker files simply ride the proposed settlement tiers [3Qxw8dtCCns @ 00:09:14].

PFAS timing calls split badly, and the record shows who ran early. Smith pegged the start of Q2 as the quarter for PFAS clarity, reasoning that the hard filing deadline finally showed defendants like 3M exactly how many claimants they would have to pay [IHvCfh-WJ6E @ 00:04:38]. Robert King of King Law, working up thousands of water contamination files, said in June that a July or August 2026 settlement would not be a surprise, tracking roughly a year of case management orders from Judge Gergel [aOm5hBG6t9s @ 00:05:03]. The deal landed in November instead, and Fantini called the roughly $7.35 billion settlement covering 115,000 to 120,000 personal injury claims pretty surprising [08ES8nUZRYk @ 00:00:39]. Michael Stanisci pushes cash expectations out further than any headline implies: no plaintiff payments in 2026, none in 2027, maybe some in the second half of 2028, then a rolling run through 2029 and 2030, because a defendant will not pay $7 billion upfront and instead pays tranche by tranche once releases and proof clear, exactly as Stanisci saw in Bard hernia mesh. Every case still has to clear the special master and the defendants. Stanisci's rule of thumb is at least a year and a half from settlement to actual funds [_qBek9AFPiI @ 00:00:35].

Intake criteria are where firm playbooks diverge most. Smith says the PFAS case management order capped the docket at six qualifying injuries, four backed by large epi studies plus two that the plaintiff side added without a Daubert ruling, and that a Daubert win on those plus two would hand plaintiffs leverage to demand more value [-H3O5pPP-XA @ 00:09:19]. Elizabeth of Lawsuit Tracker reports that some firms still sign tier 2 injuries, especially prostate cancer, on the view that it is the next injury the judge allows even with no official order, and says the Lawsuit Tracker firm screens on 40 years of latency from exposure to diagnosis while other firms run different criteria [tVouqZmWW5I @ 00:01:19]. Andrew Kroner of Napoli Shkolnik reads the next chapter as individual PFAS personal injury claims not tied directly to AFFF, with the MDL's proof requirements setting the roadmap and courts that may keep building barriers that narrow who qualifies [S1VC15_WonY @ 00:00:46]. On social media addiction, Fantini sizes the eventual docket at 200,000 to 250,000 plaintiffs against under 10,000 pending now, and holds both positions at once: there is plenty of time to get involved, yet urgency has increased significantly after the $375 million and $6 million verdicts [DQ8EXxoteKo @ 00:03:54].

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The costliest self-inflicted wound in PFAS was inventory bloat. Smith says roughly 60,000 to 70,000 cases were expected, but 131,000 were filed by the deadline; the judge was completely disgusted, Smith calls the number obscene, and the first trial, the main pressure point for a resolution, got postponed, turning the year into cleanup of dual rep issues, medical record qualifications, and exposure proof [-H3O5pPP-XA @ 00:07:44]. In the earlier segment Smith adds that loss of consortium claimants padded the count and upset the judge [IHvCfh-WJ6E @ 00:04:56]. King describes the grind that followed: Case Management Order 37 set minimum standards for plaintiff fact sheets submitted into a portal, four deficiency rounds have already run, and a fifth round attacking exposure is expected, with exposure proven through firefighter work history or residency in a contaminated system mapped by PWSID or ZIP code [aOm5hBG6t9s @ 00:04:28]. Kroner of Napoli Shkolnik warns the bar is concrete: believing you were exposed and generally knowing you have a PFAS-linked condition is not enough, and an ulcerative colitis client treated by multiple providers over years may lack the pathology reports, diagnostic imaging, treatment histories, and specialist evaluations courts want to keep a case viable [S1VC15_WonY @ 00:02:15].

Settlement mechanics punish firms that lose touch with clients. Fantini says the uncapped $5.5 billion talc deal carries a 95% participation threshold across about 70,000 cancer cases, and firms face a monumental chase because people have moved and many have passed away, so a potential rep must be submitted or the client can be excluded, an uphill spot since two of the main plaintiff experts withdrew their opinions before the deal was announced [NHmq2W3F_do @ 00:05:45]. Stanisci lists the paperwork that stalls a 100,000-claimant payout: multiple signed documents, deceased plaintiffs who need an estate and the proper party, prior bankruptcies, and approval by the special master and ultimately the defendants [_qBek9AFPiI @ 00:00:17]. Deadlines compound the drag. In Depo-Provera, Judge Rodgers created an administrative docket for settlement-only filings, while any case outside the criteria or opting out must hit the regular docket by November 30th and comply with a Lone Pine order demanding the fact sheet and an expert report [NHmq2W3F_do @ 00:07:58]. In the Missouri Roundup class, an opt-out needs an original wet signature, not DocuSign, plus a copy of ID and case-specific requirements inside 90 days, or the file is included in the settlement by default [3Qxw8dtCCns @ 00:07:40].

The economics checks run against the hype. Smith calls the Roundup class numbers bad: an average near $70,000, about $40,000 for residential use, a 10-tier grid from roughly $165,000 down to $10,000, with Bayer getting 5 years to pay and a 16-year latency tail that keeps it paying for 21 years. Smith notes Bayer separately paid a premium to a handful of firms outside the deal, which is why the litigating partner matters as much as the tort [IHvCfh-WJ6E @ 00:01:52]. Smith also flags saturation: Depo-Provera carried over a 5x increased risk against the 2x rule of thumb, yet by mid last year the market could not produce a good claimant because most were already signed [-H3O5pPP-XA @ 00:15:58]. On Camp Lejeune, Fantini puts the first bench trial demand at a little under $11 million against roughly a $500,000 value through the EO, a gap that has defense pushing a Lone Pine order while plaintiffs push a census of the 25 injuries [ql3WYzhinZk @ 00:04:06]. Trial risk cuts the other way too: in Bard PowerPort, the first infection trial deadlocked and the second came back a defense verdict, while fracture-migration cases stayed strong behind a $40 million verdict [08ES8nUZRYk @ 00:06:23].

callout.title: Four Checks Before a File Counts as Inventory
callout.body: Each check below comes from a pitfall practitioners hit on live dockets: deficiency purges, unreachable clients, botched opt-outs, and cash-flow models built on headline settlement dates.
items: Paper every PFAS file before it counts: proof of injury from medical records ordered across providers and years, plus exposure via firefighter work history or residency mapped by PWSID or ZIP code [King Law — aOm5hBG6t9s @ 00:03:52].

Refresh client contact data and line up estate reps now; talc firms are chasing moved and deceased claimants to reach a 95% threshold, and excluded clients face an uphill fight [Jon and Marc — NHmq2W3F_do @ 00:05:45].
Run Roundup opt-outs on original wet signatures, not DocuSign, with ID inside the 90-day window or the file is swept into the class [Jon and Marc — 3Qxw8dtCCns @ 00:07:40].
Budget cash flow on at least a year and a half from settlement to first funds, paid in rolling tranches after releases and proof clear [Michael Stanisci — _qBek9AFPiI @ 00:00:35].

chapters.pull_quote: "Who you litigate your cases with is everything in the landscaping of mass torts today." Steve Smith, Cut to the Chase Network (IHvCfh-WJ6E @ 00:03:23).
action_checklist: Submit the full AFFF ID order in the portal for every case you believe belongs in the settlement, then work de-duping, injury proof, and address-and-date verification for water cases [Jon and Marc — 08ES8nUZRYk @ 00:01:19].
Order medical records from every provider across the years and map each water client to a known contaminated system by PWSID or ZIP code [King Law — aOm5hBG6t9s @ 00:04:07].
Review Roundup medical records, slot each client into the proposed tier, and personally counsel recurrence or heavy-chemo clients on opting out [Jon and Marc — 3Qxw8dtCCns @ 00:08:13].
For spinal cord stimulator intake, pull the product ID from the implant sticker log and operative report to pick the right manufacturer MDL [Jon and Marc — NHmq2W3F_do @ 00:03:22].

Screen hair relaxer files for years of use, a named brand in the case, and a documented uterine, ovarian, or endometrial cancer diagnosis, and walk clients through fact sheets with genuine empathy [Salenger, Sack, Kimmel & Bavaro, LLP — ch5IVo6DOos @ 00:05:33] [Michael Stanisci — 9fbIhuuhgGE @ 00:03:25].

Qualify social media addiction claimants who started before 16, used platforms hours a week, and developed any mental health issue from anxiety and depression up to suicidal thoughts [LexHive Podcast (Formerly- The Legal Growth Lab) — DQ8EXxoteKo @ 00:07:27].

chapters.question_prompt: How do firms and affiliates generate mass-tort leads and control cost per signed case?
chapters.title: Mass-Tort Lead Generation & Acquisition Economics
chapters.subtitle: Optimal moments to seek clients, CPSC research, AI-driven lead scoring, affiliate and SMS campaigns, Google Ads agency pitfalls, cost-per-acquisition breakdowns, vendor feedback loops, barratry risks, and building settlement-ready inventory
chapters.executive_summary: Mass-tort operators agree that the signed retainer is the wrong finish line. The number that matters is cost per retained, settlement-ready case, and timing, audience size, filter alignment and the call center set it more than raw lead price does. Blue Sky Legal reports signed cases ranging from $300 early to six grand or more on crowded torts like Camp Lejeune. Devin Downey warns that a fully vetted $3,000 case is not the reality and that attrition runs 20-40%. John Casto works 3-4% raw-lead-to-retainer conversion against payouts swinging from $1,000 to $2,500, and JP Diaz runs SMS at $3-4 EPC. The disagreements are about three things: broad funnels versus narrow inverted funnels, buying vendor leads versus owning the ad account, and how strict brand and diagnosis criteria should be before signing.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner who spoke on economics lands in the same place: the signed retainer is a checkpoint, not the asset. Rob Parker of Nexus Legal Group says cases commonly die roughly 18 months in over missing proof of use, a diagnosis outside the criteria, or an endless records chase. A deficient file costs you twice, because time to payment is set by your files [4LdL5Q6T7ds @ 00:00:00]. Devin Downey puts numbers on the leak. Attrition ran about 30% from 2020 to 2024, with 20-40% treated as normal, and one source fell out at double the rate of another, so the only honest denominator is cost per retained case [My_I0OLHPXc @ 00:04:39]. TortShark frames the same rule as docket value: it doesn't matter how many cases sit on the docket if none of them settle, so viability and settlement value outrank raw count [7Jbuob_1a-Y @ 00:00:15]. On the affiliate side, John Casto reaches the identical conclusion from the media seat. The call center is going to dictate your actual cost per retainer, not just the cost per lead, so the intake floor, not the media buyer, sets the real price [Tt2FvNxVuCs @ 00:17:14]. The baseline prerequisite is a firm that measures downstream, not at the click.

The second point of agreement is that entry timing sets both price and risk. Susan Barfield and Chris Princess of Case Works map a multi-year life cycle with three entry moments: emerging, scaling and pre-settlement. Early inventory comes at an attractive price, faces little competition and can back a bid for leadership, but it carries more unknowns. The mature stage trades lower risk for higher prices and fewer available cases [or3TWPA-tro @ 00:05:08]. Serena of Blue Sky Legal attaches dollar figures to that curve: $300-$1,800 CPA on early torts with no ads running, 4K-plus once an MDL forms, and Camp Lejeune topping six grand in late 2023 [n9AQhSIMkNg @ 00:01:01]. Blue Sky's PFAS breakdown applies the same logic to a tort with established science and active litigation. That means more ads, more noise and more competition, and if you're late to launch, your CPA is already inflated [QMnpIcISv3o @ 00:00:41]. Casto watches the same decay from the affiliate side: retainer payouts swing between $1,000 and $2,500, and CPL climbs within weeks as competitors pile into a new tort [Tt2FvNxVuCs @ 00:13:15]. Across all four, the cheapest inventory belongs to whoever moves before the crowd and accepts the uncertainty that comes with it.

Third, operators agree the screening rules have to be the firm's actual signing rules, enforced before media money is spent. Rob Parker builds the vendor screen directly from the firm's criteria: proof of use, injury definitions, date ranges and record standards. Qualification happens up front, not at registration [4LdL5Q6T7ds @ 00:01:14]. Serena calls the usual complaint a misdiagnosis: the problem is not lead quality, it's filter alignment. If your intake team won't sign the people the campaign is bringing in, it's not working. Early Hernia Mesh signed at 50%, while tightly filtered Camp Lejeune converted in the six-to-8% range [n9AQhSIMkNg @ 00:01:24]. Bill Barfield says the industry has already crossed this bridge. Ten to fifteen years ago firms took everything, and today strict criteria cost more per lead but yield more compensable cases at the end of the line [AVLtP9ONXaY @ 00:15:17]. Records sit underneath all of it. Case Works vets every firm's records vendor with the same scrutiny it gives the acquisition vendor, on the blunt rule that no records means no case. A signed client with no retrievable chart never reaches the payout [or3TWPA-tro @ 00:10:02]. The prerequisite stack every speaker implies is criteria first, records path second, media third.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The Leads Warehouse lays out a three-tier product menu. The top tier is the signed case or full intake: the retainer is already executed, and the price is considerably higher because much of the intake work is done. Long-form leads capture diagnosis, prescription history and timelines. Co-reg real-time leads scale cheaply but need heavier filtering [FlPOncTNHp0 @ 00:00:54]. Devin Downey prices the top tier bluntly: a fully vetted case at $3,000 is not the reality, so expect roughly double. The choice is between the Walmart model, cheaper with more fallout, and the Neiman Marcus model, pricier with less [My_I0OLHPXc @ 00:08:14]. The bottom tier has its own cost stack: a $2 co-reg lead plus about $5 of call-center coaching before it becomes anything sellable [My_I0OLHPXc @ 00:15:47]. Casto shows why the arithmetic breaks for affiliates. An aggregator paid $400-500 per retainer on one tort, and at a three-to-5% conversion rate on a $30 cost per lead, the math doesn't always add up. The payout only rose to about $1,500 as CPL climbed [Tt2FvNxVuCs @ 00:12:42]. Every tier therefore has to be judged on what it costs after the phones and the filters, never on the sticker price.

For cheap demand, two operators teach very different street plays. Bill Hauser works the CPSC recall feed. Check cpsc.gov/recalls, ideally weekly, and skip anything with zero injuries, such as a heat pump with 6 reports and 0 injuries. Then hunt for recalls that pair high unit counts with high injury counts [mr9VmqdCZ6M @ 00:01:08]. A brand-new tort carries no keyword data, so you guess the search terms and launch a national Google Ads campaign on phrases like gordon folding knives lawsuit, where CPC is low and no rival bidders show up in the auction [mr9VmqdCZ6M @ 00:03:29]. JP Diaz of Consumer Awareness Group runs a model of calling leads, signing retainers and selling those retainers to attorneys, and mines inventory others discarded. A 3M partner was earning $300 per lead, so JP re-called aged records with wider injury criteria and more states. Those 3,000 records turned into $40,000, with 11,000 records still sitting undialed [dlxuHtoqmYw @ 00:09:32]. On text, JP pegs what you can expect at $3-4 EPC per SMS. Textria carries roughly 30 mass-tort clients, each pushing 3-4M texts per day through the channel [dlxuHtoqmYw @ 00:10:18].

Before a dollar goes into media, Blue Sky Legal runs a pre-launch competition check on the Facebook Ad Library, Google Trends and search auctions. When 30-50 firms are bidding on one tort, Blue Sky treats it as a price war, because more noise equals higher CPA [n9AQhSIMkNg @ 00:01:45]. Channel selection follows the tort's stage and criteria [n9AQhSIMkNg @ 00:02:04]:
- **Meta** is great early, but CPA spikes fast.
- **TikTok** suits buzzy cases, not complex criteria.
- **CTV and TV** buy reach at a premium.
- **Google Search** delivers high intent but turns most expensive when crowded.

Austin of Grow My Ads, who has managed over 60 million in spend, quantifies the search side. Lawyer terms run three, four, $500 per click, and anyone who doesn't know what they're doing can burn a credit card very quickly and end up with nothing [sehjNBEeVbw @ 00:04:49]. The fix Austin teaches is conversion hygiene: stop counting 30-second calls as conversions and upgrade the conversion signal toward signed-case quality. Whatever you train Google on and define as success, Google will end up getting you more of that [sehjNBEeVbw @ 00:21:42]. The media buyer's job is to feed intake signable people, not to manufacture dashboard conversions.

callout.title: Margin Protection Moves From The Acquisition Floor
callout.body: Small operational habits that operators credit with keeping cost per retained case in line.
items: Run email/phone congruence checks and TrustedForm on every lead before it reaches workup. Workup is the largest cost in the chain, so bad leads should die before it [Case Works — My_I0OLHPXc @ 00:06:57].
Control paid-social spend with bid caps and cost caps, and test across multiple ad accounts instead of trusting a single account's delivery [Advanced Affiliate — Tt2FvNxVuCs @ 00:35:02].
Frame SMS lists as lawsuit club newsletters. JP Diaz reports low complaint rates on those, versus high complaint rates on subprime and sweepstakes clubs [OfferVault — dlxuHtoqmYw @ 00:11:23].

Put a video in the email subject line for client communication. Bill Barfield reports about an 85% open rate, which keeps signed clients engaged long before settlement [Case Works — AVLtP9ONXaY @ 00:11:02].

sop_steps.title: Scout And Stage The Tort
sop_steps.action: Pull candidate torts and place each in the emerging, scaling or pre-settlement bucket before pricing anything.
sop_steps.detail: Check cpsc.gov/recalls weekly and drop recalls with zero injuries [Bill Hauser with SMB Team — mr9VmqdCZ6M @ 00:00:22]. Then decide whether the firm is buying emerging, scaling or pre-settlement inventory, since seasoned firms invest across all three buckets [Case Works — or3TWPA-tro @ 00:15:07].

sop_steps.title: Size The Audience And The Auction
sop_steps.action: Measure the exposed population and scan competitor ad activity before setting a budget.
sop_steps.detail: Ask how many people were exposed, took the drug or lived in the area. Targeting only four states or excluding key states shrinks the pool, raises CPM and can double CPA [Blue Sky Legal — n9AQhSIMkNg @ 00:00:41]. Review the Facebook Ad Library, search auction trends and tort saturation weekly [Blue Sky Legal — QMnpIcISv3o @ 00:01:01].

sop_steps.title: Lock Criteria, Volume And Price In Writing
sop_steps.action: Convert the firm's signing criteria into vendor screening rules and fix monthly volume and pricing before launch.
sop_steps.detail: Match monthly volume to the firm's intake and capital, and put pricing in writing before launch. That lets the firm compare acquisition cost against qualification rate, with no surprise add-ons [Nexus Legal Group — 4LdL5Q6T7ds @ 00:01:34].

sop_steps.title: Scale On Retained-Case Economics
sop_steps.action: Scale or cut sources on trailing conversion and cost per retained case, not on today's CPL alone.
sop_steps.detail: Scale on today's CPL plus the last seven to 14 days of conversion rate and cost per retainer [Advanced Affiliate — Tt2FvNxVuCs @ 00:18:41]. Re-rank sources on cost per retained case, because one source can fall out at twice another's rate [Case Works — My_I0OLHPXc @ 00:04:39].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split among operators is how tight to set the intake net. Susan Barfield and Chris Princess of Case Works describe two camps: firms that run a traditional funnel, sign wide and cull later, and firms that run an inverted funnel with narrow criteria from day one [or3TWPA-tro @ 00:08:04]. Bill Barfield sits squarely in the narrow camp, arguing that strict criteria cost more per lead but yield more compensable cases, and contrasting it with ten to fifteen years ago when firms simply took everything [AVLtP9ONXaY @ 00:15:17]. John Casto, buying traffic as an affiliate, reports the opposite result from the media side: bolting a DQ filter onto a campaign doubled his CPL with no lift in conversion off a typical 3-4% raw-lead-to-retainer rate [Tt2FvNxVuCs @ 00:14:53]. Ben Martin hit the same wall from the attorney chair. A brand-confirmation requirement at intake had his team rejecting hundreds of valid Depo-Provera cases, so he dropped it and now verifies brand through the medical records instead [AyY5OoT74DQ @ 00:29:07]. The split is less about strictness than about where each filter gets enforced: Barfield enforces criteria before the sign, Martin moves the hardest proof point downstream to the records pull, and Casto refuses to pay media dollars for filters that do not move retainers.

The second fault line is what a firm should actually buy. The Leads Warehouse lays out three products: signed cases with an executed retainer that 'cost considerably more' because intake is done, long-form leads capturing diagnosis, prescription history and timelines, and co-reg real-time leads that scale cheaply but need heavier filtering [FlPOncTNHp0 @ 00:00:54]. Devin Downey frames the same choice as the 'Walmart model', cheaper per case with more fallout, versus the 'Neiman Marcus model', which costs more and holds better, and he warns that a fully vetted case at $3,000 is 'not the reality' when double is closer [My_I0OLHPXc @ 00:08:51]. Serena at Blue Sky Legal rejects the lead market outright: 'We don't sell leads,' she says, positioning the shop as an end-to-end retainer delivery operation covering creative, filters, intake scripting, HIPAA and document collection [QMnpIcISv3o @ 00:01:21]. Kaylee on Legal Lead Sharks goes further toward ownership, comparing lead buying to funding someone else's retirement account because every purchased lead trains a vendor's machine instead of the firm's own [zELnyJbIEGM @ 00:13:37]. Jimmy Goff's cost logic backs her: the same money spent on a direct agency avoids a $50k barratry fine, lost fees and a bar report.

Timing and channel split the field a third way. Case Works pitches early entry as the low-competition, attractively priced window where inventory can back a leadership bid, accepting more unknowns, while the mature stage brings less risk, higher prices and fewer cases; Chris Princess notes new firms usually pick middle-tier torts and pay more per case, while seasoned firms buy into all three buckets [or3TWPA-tro @ 00:15:07]. Serena puts numbers on the curve: $300-$1,800 CPA on early torts with no ads running, 4K+ once an MDL forms, and Camp Lejeune topping six grand in late 2023 [n9AQhSIMkNg @ 00:01:01]. Bill Hauser plays the earliest edge of all, mining cpsc.gov recalls weekly for high unit and injury counts, then running national Google Ads on terms like 'gordon folding knives lawsuit' where CPC is low and nobody else is bidding [mr9VmqdCZ6M @ 00:03:29]. On channel, JP Diaz calls Facebook expensive and SMS cheap and legal, quoting $3-$4 EPC on texts, while Serena ranks Meta great early but quick to spike, TikTok good for buzzy cases rather than complex criteria, CTV for premium reach, and Google Search the most expensive once crowded [dlxuHtoqmYw @ 00:07:43].

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive failure practitioners report firsthand is buying claimants who do not exist. Ben Martin says prior vendors delivered Depo-Provera claimants who never took the drug or never had a meningioma, putting it bluntly: 'The folks that they're signing up are not real people' [AyY5OoT74DQ @ 00:16:56]. The tell arrived only a few months in, as clients went unreachable and refused basic information requests, and Sebastian Westerby's answer is six onshore intake agents, deliberately not offshore, with QA before handoff. JP Diaz traces the duplicate-case problem to incentivized call centers dangling $500 Walmart gift cards, and says Mass Torts Made Perfect will circulate a fraud hit list of agencies and affiliates [dlxuHtoqmYw @ 00:05:40]. Devin Downey pins dual representation to the very start of the relationship, reporting clients signed with eight or nine firms on opioids and five or six on Camp Lejeune [My_I0OLHPXc @ 00:10:18]. Ron Lasorsa adds the liability layer: if the firm cannot prove the consumer initiated contact, the firm carries the solicitation exposure, which is why he presses buyers to know the generation process and the vendor's true cost to generate [mmpH5piuvUk @ 00:00:49].

The second trap is treating a signed retainer as finished inventory. Rob Parker at Nexus Legal Group says files commonly die around 18 months in on missing proof of use, a diagnosis outside the criteria or a records chase, and that a deficient file 'costs you twice' [4LdL5Q6T7ds @ 00:00:00]. Downey measured roughly 30% attrition from 2020 to 2024, calls 20-40% normal, and watched one source fall out at twice the rate of another, which is why he prices on cost per retained case rather than cost per sign [My_I0OLHPXc @ 00:04:39]. He adds that Camp Lejeune, the largest direct-response campaign ever, produced 2023 signs that retained poorly. On the seller side, John Casto had one buyer return four of 12 retainers at roughly $2,800 each in a single day, sees dispositions arrive two to three days late, and watched a large firm return retainers after 30 days against a typical 14-day window [Tt2FvNxVuCs @ 00:18:02]. Bill Barfield traces no-records-found outcomes to wrong date ranges, the wrong pharmacy, Walmart versus Walgreens, and the 7-year retention limit, and his audits of 10,000-plus dormant cases kept surfacing dual reps [AVLtP9ONXaY @ 00:17:41].

The third failure class is paying for activity that never becomes a case. Jimmy Goff burned $25,000 on Facebook ads in his first year on a coaching group's push, and the Legal Lead Sharks crew cite a $200,000 agency engagement that delivered no cases at all [zELnyJbIEGM @ 00:10:33]. Austin of Grow My Ads lists the agency red flags: 30-second phone calls counted as conversions, vanity metrics, 20-page reports and PMax running in a PI account where click-to-sign can take 48 hours [sehjNBEeVbw @ 00:21:09]. His rule is that whatever you define as success, Google gets you more of, so the conversion definition must be upgraded toward signed quality. Devin Downey's vendor screen asks whether media buyers are on staff, whether hidden DC or Arizona ABS law-firm relationships sit behind the vendor, and how clean the handoff to the firm is, since weak handoffs breed attrition [My_I0OLHPXc @ 00:19:49]. Even inside a scaling firm, Thaddeus Wendt admits the breakdown was execution, not design: 'We had the awesome people not using our awesome SOPs,' and Feller & Wendt answered by standing up a QA department run by a former Treasury auditor [My1QKQ-hGSw @ 00:19:37].

callout.title: Gate Every Source Before You Scale It
callout.body: Four checks built from losses practitioners took firsthand on fake claimants, attrition, retainer returns and solicitation exposure.
items: Hold judgment on any new vendor until intake confirms clients are reachable and answer basic information requests; unreachable clients and refusals were the fraud tell a few months in [Tort Experts — AyY5OoT74DQ @ 00:21:03].
Price every source on cost per retained case, not cost per sign, because one source fell out at twice the rate of another [Case Works — My_I0OLHPXc @ 00:04:39].
Scale on today's CPL plus the trailing seven-to-14-day conversion rate and cost per retainer, and budget for returns landing past the 14-day window [Advanced Affiliate — Tt2FvNxVuCs @ 00:18:41].

Require proof the consumer initiated contact and know the vendor's generation process and true cost to generate before buying, since the firm carries the solicitation exposure [Ron Lasorsa — mmpH5piuvUk @ 00:00:49].

chapters.pull_quote: "It doesn't matter how many cases you have on the docket if none of them actually settle." — attributed to tortshark (7Jbuob_1a-Y @ 00:00:15).
action_checklist: Check cpsc.gov/recalls weekly, skip recalls with zero injuries, and prioritize high unit counts and high injury counts before guessing search terms for a national Google Ads test [Bill Hauser with SMB Team — mr9VmqdCZ6M @ 00:01:08].
Before launching any campaign, check the Facebook Ad Library, Google Trends and search auctions; 30-50 firms bidding means a price war [Blue Sky Legal — n9AQhSIMkNg @ 00:01:45].

Turn the firm's own criteria (proof of use, injury definitions, date ranges, record standards) into screening rules and lock pricing in writing before launch [Nexus Legal Group — 4LdL5Q6T7ds @ 00:01:14].
Validate incoming leads with email/phone congruence and TrustedForm, and confirm the vendor has media buyers on staff [Case Works — My_I0OLHPXc @ 00:06:57].

Engage clients from the start through their preferred channel, using a video in the email subject line for roughly an 85% open rate, never waiting until settlement [Case Works — AVLtP9ONXaY @ 00:11:02].
Run tickers and scheduled contact and keep current address, email and phone data on every client to plug the attrition leak [Tort Experts — AyY5OoT74DQ @ 00:32:22].

chapters.question_prompt: How do firms convert leads into signed clients and keep them informed throughout a mass tort?
chapters.title: Intake, Conversion & Client Communication
chapters.subtitle: Intake scripts and call patching, AI voice agents and Intake EQ, Litify questionnaires and qualification, converting mass-tort leads, the client journey, MDL communication expectations, and shared-cost explanations
chapters.executive_summary: Mass tort intake operators agree the money leaks at the phone, not the ad. Saad Khan says missing a 60-second callback cuts conversion by over 70%. Alert Communications wants outbound contact within 1 to 3 minutes and reports a 5x drop inside 5 minutes for injured callers. K'Lee Terrazas cites a Google report showing 28% of Google Business Profile calls missed on the first attempt. Alert's floor converts 70% of leads into qualified leads and says broken intake converts only 20% to 40%. The mechanics include 3-ring overflow ladders, redials at varied times that lift contact to 75% to 80%, tort-specific questionnaires that grew from 4 to 50 questions, and retainers e-signed while the caller is still on the line. Practitioners split on AI agents at $1 per minute versus 24/7 human answering. They also split on Harvard's one-hour response window, which Alert calls too long.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator in this chapter lands on the same diagnosis: the money leaks at the phone, not the ad. Saad Khan prices one mass tort lead at up to $3,000 against a $4,000 signed retainer. Khan says missing a 60-second callback drops conversion by over 70%, so the problem is speed to lead, not bad ads [ZkN7hMCBwmQ @ 00:00:00]. Alert Communications runs a 425-seat intake floor and sets the bar at an outbound call within 1 to 3 minutes. Alert says the loss turns significant after 5 minutes, and that injured callers show a fivefold drop inside that window [PJEVefyQCxA @ 00:22:15]. K'Lee Terrazas backs the same point with a Google report showing 28% of Google Business Profile calls go unanswered on the first attempt [XcpDdsuGoEY @ 00:03:27]. Terrazas is blunt about what happens next: those callers are not going to leave a voicemail [j80F3HgdRAw @ 00:03:15]. All three treat round-the-clock coverage as the baseline prerequisite. Khan sells an always-on workflow that answers every channel, Alert staffs around the clock, and Terrazas pitches an agent that never burns out at 5 p.m. A firm that buys TV, radio, or paid search traffic without that coverage pays full price for leads it will never reach, and then blames the media vendor.

The second point of agreement is that intake is a sales function and should be judged like one. Tony Prito and Nick Worker of Answering Legal say marketers take the blame when the P&L shows no cases, even though intake is the real gap. They state flatly that the first consultation with a prospective client is a sales call, and that the motive is helping the caller, not chasing money [2az9KaozXKQ @ 00:16:30]. Alert Communications goes further. Alert says the intake manager is really a sales manager, and that firms with broken intake convert 20% to 40% of leads instead of the 70% to 80% a tuned operation delivers [PJEVefyQCxA @ 00:16:47]. Andrew Picket's Melbourne and Titusville firm has recovered about $38 million at a 95% settlement rate. Picket tells operators to record every call, honoring two-party consent where it applies, and to audit intake before spending another dollar on marketing [lW3uPdauQrA @ 00:29:07]. Host K'Lee Terrazas underlines the cost of skipping that audit with the story of a $500 click that could have been a million-dollar case, lost at intake [lW3uPdauQrA @ 00:30:22]. The shared rule: the intake desk is the conversion engine for the whole acquisition budget. Staff it with closers, script it like a sales floor, and measure it before blaming the media buy.

The third consensus is that client communication does not stop at the signed retainer, because the long middle of a mass tort is where clients drift. Lawsuit Tracker explains that once the attorney submits the very detailed case information sheet, little happens on an individual MDL case until bellwethers, settlement, or remand. That is why the question asked most often is what is going on with my individual case [WmvLnQq2ZuY @ 00:00:29]. Chaffin Luhana answers it with a deliberate client journey. The firm assigns each client a team of lawyers, paralegals, and assistants, then walks the client through case development, record review, litigation, settlement, and an itemized disbursement of every penny, so there are no surprises [5cou1UWhrYw @ 00:00:02]. Maury Goldstein of Aylstock Witkin Kreis & Overholtz frames the stakes in money terms: staying connected through settlement is how clients get paid and how the firm earns a return on its acquisition spend [kjUaKK45Ahg @ 00:00:04]. Answering Legal adds that lack of communication is the number one bar complaint, and positions a 24/7 human answering service as the reassurance layer [2az9KaozXKQ @ 00:20:09]. Silence during the MDL is predictable, so operators agree the communication system has to be built before the silence starts.

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Alert Communications runs a specific response ladder. An inbound call rings no more than 3 times, then plays a recorded message, holds for no longer than 15 seconds, and rolls to the overflow center. Alert built the ladder this way because abandonment climbs after 3 rings and after a 15-second hold. One firm had callers waiting on hold for 6 minutes [PJEVefyQCxA @ 00:21:02]. Web leads get an instant text, then a call and an email. On callbacks, Alert reports that immediate dials reach 37% to 40% of leads, while repeating attempts at varied times of day lifts contact to 75% to 80% [PJEVefyQCxA @ 00:35:45]. Saad Khan automates the first rung with event-driven injection, which fires an outbound call within milliseconds of a form fill. Khan claims a 391% boost from first-minute contact and runs ingestion, routing, qualification, data structuring, and CRM sync with no human in the loop [ZkN7hMCBwmQ @ 00:01:09]. Inside the CRM, Litify trainers show how to catch leads that slip through. Build a party list view filtered by last-called date so unreachable intakes surface for another attempt, then pin and clone that view for daily cleanup [5eCAkl3wUBg @ 00:19:48]. Every tool here applies the same rule: no lead sits untouched, and every missed contact goes back into a queue.

Screening scripts start short when a tort is new and get longer as it matures. Alert Communications says its 3M earplug intake started at 4 questions in early 2019 and grew to 50 by the late stage, and that intake should be re-customized monthly [PJEVefyQCxA @ 00:30:58]. Saad Khan's AI agent applies MDL screens automatically: a jurisdictional baseline, a 30-day exposure minimum, and a 1953 to 1987 date range. Non-qualifiers are auto-rejected with no paralegal needed, and complex cases go to a human review queue [ZkN7hMCBwmQ @ 00:01:27]. Litify builds one questionnaire per case type, branching like a Choose Your Own Adventure book. CQC rules auto-turn-down cases that fail, answers auto-map to record fields, and output can be downloaded as a PDF or emailed [5eCAkl3wUBg @ 00:39:38]. K'Lee Terrazas's demo agent, Kim, walks a personal injury caller through eleven steps in a fixed order: name and phone, callback permission, self or someone else, accident date, treatment, other attorney, city and state, fault, description, injuries, and ER or clinic. Kim then pitches no fees upfront and offers a live transfer [XcpDdsuGoEY @ 00:00:47]. In every version, screening produces structured, reportable fields that drive auto-rejection, routing, and CRM sync, instead of free-text notes someone has to re-read later.

Closing and unit economics are where the numbers get hard. Alert Communications closes in a strict order. First, stay on the call and text the retainer for e-signature. Next, email it. Only then mail packets, which older hernia mesh claimants needed but 3M military claimants almost never did [PJEVefyQCxA @ 00:37:21]. Alert's cost model puts cost per acquisition at $2,000, with $500 to $1,750 going to marketing and $250 to $500 to intake, and each lost lead costing up to $750 [PJEVefyQCxA @ 00:17:17]. On answering cost, K'Lee Terrazas quotes AI agents at $1 per minute for 1,000 minutes or less, against $2 to $5 per minute for call centers. After 3 years in the industry, Terrazas calls that call-center service subpar [e67Bx9d5FBc @ 00:00:46]. Modern Legal Ops split its pipeline into open, working, under review, and retainer response. The team then tracked time-to-touch, open-to-offer, time under review, and open-to-close, segmented by investor claims, class action, mass tort, and assigned attorney. The slowdown turned out to be internal attorney workup, not the intake agent [jycz9TsdE9w @ 00:01:16]. The takeaway is to price every rung of the funnel and time every handoff, because the bottleneck often sits after intake has already done its job.

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is over how fast is fast enough. Saad Khan frames the whole mass tort leak as a speed-to-lead problem, not a bad-ads problem: a lead can run up to $3,000, a signed retainer $4,000, and missing a 60-second callback drops conversion by over 70% [ZkN7hMCBwmQ @ 00:00:00]. The Khan build fires an outbound call within milliseconds through event-driven injection and claims a 391% boost from first-minute contact [ZkN7hMCBwmQ @ 00:01:09]. Alert Communications runs a human floor and sets a looser but still brutal bar: outbound dial within one to three minutes, with significant loss after five [PJEVefyQCxA @ 00:22:15]. Alert cites the InsideSales/MIT numbers, 12,700 reached in the first hour versus 1,190 later, and a 5x drop within five minutes for injured callers [PJEVefyQCxA @ 00:23:00]. Where Alert breaks openly with the research is the Harvard finding that leads are 7x more likely to qualify within one hour; the speaker's verdict is that one hour is too long because the claimant signs elsewhere [PJEVefyQCxA @ 00:23:57]. So the operator choice is between a sub-second machine dial and a one-to-three-minute human dial, and nobody on either side defends a sixty-minute window.

The second fight is machine versus human on the phones. K'Lee Terrazas pitches AI intake agents at $1 a minute for a thousand minutes or less, against the $2 to $5 a minute that call centers charge for what Terrazas calls subpar service, based on three years in the industry [e67Bx9d5FBc @ 00:00:46]. Terrazas argues traditional centers never learned the Google Ads cadence, while AI runs 24/7 with unlimited concurrent calls, no payroll, no training, no turnover, and never hits the 5:00 p.m. burnout that human intake does [e67Bx9d5FBc @ 00:01:16]. Answering Legal takes the opposite position: the top bar complaint is lack of communication, and a live 24/7 human answering service reassures callers in a way the hosts explicitly contrast with AI automation [2az9KaozXKQ @ 00:20:09]. Alert Communications stakes out the scaled-human version, with all agents US-based, 65% bilingual, and pricing by the minute in tenth increments, flat cost-per-lead, or flat rates [PJEVefyQCxA @ 00:55:20]. On the retention side, Maury Goldstein of Aylstock Witkin Kreis & Overholtz says Kayse lets two to three people handle tens of thousands of clients weekly, where the alternative was an entire department or an entire offshore development [kjUaKK45Ahg @ 00:00:47]. The trade is per-minute cost and concurrency on the AI side against human reassurance and bilingual staff on the call-center side.

After the retainer is signed, the camps split again on how much the client should hear. Lawsuit Tracker tells MDL clients bluntly that once the attorney submits the very detailed case information sheet, little happens on an individual case, and the client should track the internet, YouTube channels, and monthly or bi-monthly attorney newsletters instead [WmvLnQq2ZuY @ 00:00:29]. Andrew Picket runs the opposite playbook: every phase change in Hona triggers an automated text carrying a Picket video explaining investigation, treatment, or negotiation and settlement [lW3uPdauQrA @ 00:23:39]. On top of that, the firm ships a welcome box around day 14 with a blanket and power bank for comfort and connection, mails birthday cards, and asks outright for referrals [lW3uPdauQrA @ 00:25:26]. Chaffin Luhana builds an intentional client journey so there are no surprises, assigning each client a team of lawyers, paralegals, and assistants who learn the story, the injuries, and the life impact [5cou1UWhrYw @ 00:00:21]. Kayse users treat silence as a money problem, not a courtesy problem: Goldstein ties lifecycle contact directly to clients getting paid and the firm earning a return on its acquisition investment [kjUaKK45Ahg @ 00:00:04]. The low-touch MDL model saves staff hours; the high-touch model protects the docket from client drift.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive failure is paying for leads that intake then wastes. Saad Khan cites one firm that burned $24,000 in payroll processing 800 rejected leads, the exact cost the auto-reject screening is built to kill [ZkN7hMCBwmQ @ 00:00:15]. Alert Communications puts numbers on the conversion gap: firms with broken intake convert 20% to 40% of leads instead of 70% to 80% [PJEVefyQCxA @ 00:16:47]. Alert's worked example runs a $2,000 cost per acquisition built from $500 to $1,750 of marketing and $250 to $500 of intake, with a single lost lead costing up to $750 [PJEVefyQCxA @ 00:17:17]. The trap that hides this is an undersized funnel: a firm reporting 70 out of 100 looks healthy while the leads it never captured stay invisible, against an Alert campaign running at 70% qualified that can reach 80% to 85% [PJEVefyQCxA @ 00:14:18]. K'Lee Terrazas adds the paid-media version of the same loss: another attorney's $30,000 in Facebook ads was a 100% loss [lW3uPdauQrA @ 00:13:28]. Andrew Picket's fix is procedural, not budgetary: record every call, honoring two-party consent where it applies, and check intake before spending another dollar on marketing [lW3uPdauQrA @ 00:29:07].

The phone itself is where leads bleed out. Alert Communications measured abandonment rising after three rings and again after a 15-second hold, and reported one firm running six-minute holds [PJEVefyQCxA @ 00:19:14]. The overflow sequence Alert prescribes is three rings, a recorded message, a 15-second hold, then roll to the overflow center [PJEVefyQCxA @ 00:21:02]. Alert also found voicemail or no answer on 35% of calls, and flags paralegals juggling intake alongside other work as a weak point [PJEVefyQCxA @ 00:28:06]. Repeat-attempt data shows why one dial is never enough: immediate calls reach 37% to 40%, and varying call times lifts contact to 75% to 80% [PJEVefyQCxA @ 00:35:45]. K'Lee Terrazas cites a Google report that 28% of GBP calls were missed on the first attempt [XcpDdsuGoEY @ 00:03:27], and is blunt about what happens next: those callers are not going to leave a voicemail [j80F3HgdRAw @ 00:03:15]. Terrazas built Intake EQ after watching a $500 click that could have been a million-dollar case get lost [lW3uPdauQrA @ 00:30:22]. Even the AI fix shows seams: in the live demo, the agent Kim misnamed the caller Kaitlin versus Caitlyn while running the eleven-question PI screen.

Some failures sit downstream of the phone. Modern Legal Ops watched volume roughly double from 2024 to 2026 with a single intake agent, Lisa, while conversion lagged because three to four hidden steps sat between open and close [jycz9TsdE9w @ 00:00:00]. After splitting the pipeline into open, working, under review, and retainer response, and timing each stage, the culprit turned out to be internal attorney workup, not intake [jycz9TsdE9w @ 00:01:16]. Litify's trainer flags quieter CRM traps: a list-view search only covers that filtered list, so staff can miss intakes that exist elsewhere [5eCAkl3wUBg @ 00:11:34], and stacking too many banners on a record slows the page [5eCAkl3wUBg @ 00:23:03]. Litify's answer to the unreachable lead is a party list view filtered by last-called date [5eCAkl3wUBg @ 00:19:48]. The late-stage failure is client drift after signing. Goldstein describes thousands of Aylstock clients the firm had absolutely no hope of connecting with after exhausting every other channel, until Kayse reached 20% to 30% of them and brought them back to get paid through settlements [kjUaKK45Ahg @ 00:01:00]. Alert adds that screeners never sit still: the 3M intake grew from four questions in early 2019 to fifty late-stage, and intake gets customized monthly [PJEVefyQCxA @ 00:33:14].

chapters.question_prompt: Which case-management platforms and automations do mass-tort and PI firms use, and how are they configured?
chapters.title: The Case-Management Stack: Filevine, Litify & Automation
chapters.subtitle: Filevine projects, medical tracking and AI tools, Zapier and Workato workflows, paralegal tips, Litify basics, Harvey vs. Filevine, CaseCube/LawAccounting billing, and why small firms adopt Filevine, MyCase and Smokeball
chapters.executive_summary: Operators running mass-tort and PI volume on Filevine, Litify and Case Cube converge on one rule: the case-management platform must be the single system of record, with intake, medicals, liens, trust and settlement inside one controlled stack. LawAccounting shows a $2M IOLTA wire auto-allocated by demand into 12 receipts, a check run producing 48 checks, and fee codes that block progress unless they total 100%. Vineskills engineers price Zapier at about $30/month for 750 tasks versus roughly $3,300/month near 1M tasks at mass-tort volume, and warn that on-save triggers, loops and bulk live-environment writes burn tasks or spawn ten thousand items. Disagreement centers on walled-garden client portals, how far to trust AI chronologies, and whether native automation, Workato or Zapier comes first.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The baseline every serious operator agrees on is a single system of record. LawAccounting runs Case Cube and its trust ledger natively on Salesforce so case management and trust accounting share one source of truth, then layers role-built dashboards for attorneys, paralegals, bookkeepers and case managers on top [dqv7XkRgaQQ @ 00:00:45]. Their Mass Tort Portfolio view works as a command center that drills from docket to plaintiff group to individual matter, which is the shape a mass-tort shop needs once inventory stacks up across referring firms and settlement waves. How to Simple describes Litify the same way: a Salesforce-built platform carrying matters from intake to resolution with configurable workflows for PI, mass torts and corporate work, automated task assignment, and a CRM that fires client follow-ups [3bh0rzq79u8 @ 00:01:17]. SelectHub's Filevine-sponsored comparison draws the line sharply against AI-only layers: Harvey augments an existing system of record and offers no case management or billing, while Filevine positions itself as the operations-first record for mass torts with AI embedded throughout [RE04OZvO3RQ @ 00:03:20]. The operational takeaway is blunt. If billing and financial management are on the requirements list, SelectHub says Filevine is the only option in that matchup, and an AI drafting tool bolted onto spreadsheets cannot carry a docket or move settlement money.

The second point of agreement is that automation is only as good as the manual process underneath it. Stephanie at Vineskills, a paralegal with a workers' comp background, tells firms to exhaust Filevine's native tools first, meaning Doctrine, task flows and deadline chains, before paying for a third-party engine [YtXAzduQ3PE @ 00:02:33]. Workato's integration user holds org-admin rights only, so it can only do what a user could do by hand, and the API documentation sets the real limits. Susie Lewis, who implemented Workato inside Filevine, frames the same rule: if a user can do it, it can probably be automated, provided the logic is consistent, and every build is unique to the firm's template with no copy and paste [9_hNat-thXA @ 00:08:09]. Both push restraint. Lewis's team offers free audits and warns against stuffing a template with automations just because they sound cool, while Stephanie makes every builder answer what happens if the automation fails, because a broken deadline chain can end in the m word, malpractice [YtXAzduQ3PE @ 00:06:00]. Josh Hostilo of Filevine adds the staffing piece: hire a dedicated platform admin rather than handing the system to attorneys or paralegals, a lesson from a 97-person prior firm, and steer small firms toward managed-service consultants instead [9AejH9lLg90 @ 00:16:56].

Every practitioner who touched AI or bulk intake insists on a human checkpoint and a hard control at the front door. LawAccounting makes the conflict check mandatory on bulk intake; in their demo it flagged 4 conflicts across 4 plaintiffs that had to be dispositioned or dismissed before the CSV import would proceed, which they call scalable intake with controls intact [dqv7XkRgaQQ @ 00:04:49]. Daya Naef, a Filevine prompt engineer and former paralegal, demos AI medical chronologies that extract date of service by date of service and export to Excel, but says the output is a fairly good foundation for the work rather than a replacement for human judgment [1QCGIBQ7PQI @ 00:09:42]. Jay Stephanie of Levinson and Stefani keeps AI Fields output in its own section so the team can always tell machine work from manual work [TrEm-Mk2jeQ @ 00:14:03]. Tech Help Man, reviewing Litify's public product pages rather than a live login, calls the agentic case expert an ambitious promise and tells buyers to verify what each agent can access and change, where a person must approve, and to demo a representative workflow with human review defined before relying on AI [g6KQDADEgmI @ 00:11:20]. Clear approval rules, in their words, give each step an accountable owner.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: LawAccounting's mass-tort run is the most complete money workflow on record. Plaintiffs are grouped into cohorts by referring firm, injury type or settlement wave, such as a Camp Lejeune group, and loaded by CSV with each row mapped to a docket, group and fee code [dqv7XkRgaQQ @ 00:03:37]. The Fee Code Library splits each settlement among the primary firm, referring counsel and co-counsel, and the code must total 100%; edit one line and the 95% remainder blocks progress. The Mass Expense Allocator spread $12,000 of investigator fees across 12 matters, split equally, weighted by demand, or firm-only, and paid expenses post as disbursements while unpaid ones become payables [dqv7XkRgaQQ @ 00:06:03]. A $2M wire into IOLTA auto-allocated by demand; nudging one allocation from 175 to 170 left $500 unallocated before 12 receipts posted. The settlement check run used a $393,000 spread with a cap-override percentage and produced 48 checks, followed by pre-bill review, closing statements, e-signature, and approve-and-post-to-trust attorney remittances before bulk printing [dqv7XkRgaQQ @ 00:11:11]. On the Filevine side, David at Vineskills runs mass torts through parent/child project linking and a Lead Docket to Zapier to Filevine pipe for intake [oNoHY7832hw @ 00:29:25].

Automation cost is counted in tasks, and the engineers who build it give exact numbers. David, Vineskills' Zapier engineer for about two years and maintainer of the Filevine connector, says the connector itself is free, but the free Zapier plan likely cannot use it; the Professional plan runs about $30 a month on monthly billing for 750 tasks [oNoHY7832hw @ 00:31:13]. A case-numbering automation eats 2 to 3 tasks, so 750 tasks covers roughly 250 new cases a month, and three to five tasks is their working estimate per automation [oNoHY7832hw @ 00:32:40]. Mass-tort clients they have supported sit closer to a million tasks or more, which lands near $3,300 a month, so loops are expensive and code blocks are the lever for cutting task count. Stephanie applies the same discipline in Workato: prefer action-button or on-create triggers and avoid on-save and activity triggers that burn tasks every time someone touches a record [YtXAzduQ3PE @ 00:16:34]. Workato itself is licensed and sold through Filevine as an annual usage-based add-on bought via the account manager, per Susie Lewis, and it reaches Google Suite and custom APIs when compatible [9_hNat-thXA @ 00:01:27]. Lewis's team bills hourly and optimization blocks month to month.

For medical records and liens, the working build is a collection section with one card per provider. Jay Stephanie, whose Chicago firm has run Filevine for about five years, uses that layout so reports can sum across cards, starting with provider, treatment dates, injuries and charged amount, then adding complaints, diagnosis codes, balance owed as a lien signal, and payors, because anything you want reported has to be a field [TrEm-Mk2jeQ @ 00:01:17]. Their medical bill summary exports to Excel with a SUM formula and gets pasted into interrogatories, demands and mediation submissions; records-past-due and bills-past-due reports email to paralegals weekly [TrEm-Mk2jeQ @ 00:10:26]. Their retrieval vendor auto-uploads records into the damages and medicals folders with #MedRecs and #MedBills tags and pushes invoices into expenses. Susie Lewis automates the handoff: an Intake send-to-Medical button creates a Medical item per provider, and a lien/LOP Yes answer spawns a Lien item mapped to the lien holder, cross-linked back to its Medical card [9_hNat-thXA @ 00:19:04]. Daya Naef shows AI Fields firing on upload of a roughly 70-page record with about 10 preconfigured prompt types such as chronology, pain scores and deposition questions [1QCGIBQ7PQI @ 00:06:29]. Jay Stephanie orders records in 3-month batches and strips superfluous pages first.
