callout.title: Small Settings That Save Mass-Tort Teams Hours
callout.body: These are the field-tested moves practitioners use to keep automations contained, document productions clean, lead texting safe, and task assignments visible.
items: Fence every new recipe: set trigger conditions on section and field selectors, exclude the API user, and limit the run to a single test project ID until it is proven [Vineskills — YtXAzduQ3PE @ 00:24:15].
Combine documents first, then Bates stamp, because stamping does not combine for you; copy the original before redacting, since saved redactions are permanent [Vineskills — XAU9uhQg6nk @ 00:17:03].

Auto-text web leads with a five-minute reply promise and the number you will call from, but use keyword stops so the system never auto-replies to injury photos [Lunch Hour Legal Marketing — 9AejH9lLg90 @ 00:15:28].

Reassign only uncompleted tasks; a completed task moved to another user stays invisible on their list, so start a fresh thread from the write-a-note field instead [Errol Janusz — mfKVI7JPrYc @ 00:00:37].

sop_steps.title: Scope the automation target
sop_steps.action: Hunt for duplicate data entry and processes that work but feel manual or clunky.
sop_steps.detail: Ask where effort is duplicated, such as an incident date typed into both Intake and Case Summary, and which consistent-logic steps feel clunky, such as revealing hidden litigation sections; log each candidate with status, priority, template, impacted sections and impacted fields [Vineskills — 9_hNat-thXA @ 00:04:48].

sop_steps.title: Pick a task-efficient trigger
sop_steps.action: Use an action button or on-create trigger instead of on-save or activity triggers.
sop_steps.detail: Action-button and on-create triggers fire only when intended, while on-save and activity triggers burn tasks on every record touch; remember hidden sections cannot receive data [Vineskills — YtXAzduQ3PE @ 00:15:15].

sop_steps.title: Build in order with error handling
sop_steps.action: Sequence get project, get form, create collection item, then add an error recipe and run test recipe.
sop_steps.detail: Run the steps in order, attach an error recipe with email alerts so failures do not spam staff, rerun on a 504 timeout, and use test recipe before going live [Vineskills — YtXAzduQ3PE @ 00:31:42].

sop_steps.title: Go live and document
sop_steps.action: Remove the test project ID, notify users, note each automated field, and export the tracker.
sop_steps.detail: Strip the test project ID limit, tell users what changed, record the automation in each field's internal notes, and export the tracker collection as documentation instead of setting it and forgetting it [Vineskills — YtXAzduQ3PE @ 00:50:49].

sections.title: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The first split is where the automation layer should live. Stephanie at Vineskills tells operators to exhaust Filevine's native tooling, meaning Doctrine, task flows and deadline chains, before buying any third-party layer, and reminds them that Workato's integration user carries org-admin rights only, so it can do nothing a user could not do manually [YtXAzduQ3PE @ 00:02:33]. David, the Vineskills Zapier engineer who maintains the Filevine connector, pushes outward instead: Zapier reaches 9,000-plus apps, any API and AI blocks, the connector is free, and Lois Workflows has no external connectors yet, so Lois handles internal moves while Zapier carries traffic between systems [oNoHY7832hw @ 00:05:38]. Susie Lewis, who implemented Workato at Filevine, runs a third playbook: Workato licensed through Filevine as an annual usage-based add-on, scoped by hunting duplicated entry and clunky-but-working processes, with every recipe built unique to the firm's template and no copy-paste between clients [9_hNat-thXA @ 00:01:27]. Mass tort intake splits the same way. David names parent/child project linking or a Lead Docket to Zapier to Filevine pipe, while LawAccounting skips middleware entirely and pushes plaintiffs through a CSV import mapped row by row to docket, group and fee code, gated by a mandatory conflict check [dqv7XkRgaQQ @ 00:04:13].

Platform choice splits along Salesforce lines and along how much trust to hand the AI. How to Simple reports that Litify runs on Salesforce, offers no free trial, and quotes separate law-firm and in-house packages only through its sales team [3bh0rzq79u8 @ 00:08:39]. SelectHub, in a comparison Filevine sponsored, casts Harvey as an AI-first document layer that augments an existing system of record with no case management or billing, and Filevine as operations-first with AI embedded throughout, adding that where billing and financial management are requirements, Filevine is the only option of the two [RE04OZvO3RQ @ 00:02:22]. On AI reliance the camps diverge hardest. Daya Naef, a Filevine prompt engineer and former paralegal, says click-through citations are what built their trust in the sidebar because it is no black box, and claims there is no limit to how many records a firm can run against AI under Projects AI [1QCGIBQ7PQI @ 00:15:55]. Tech Help Man reads Litify's agentic case expert as an ambitious promise, telling buyers to verify what each agent can access and change, to locate where a person must approve, and to define human review before relying on any output [g6KQDADEgmI @ 00:10:15]. Their closing play is a demo run on a representative workflow rather than a canned tour.

The client-facing layer and the question of who owns the stack draw the sharpest open arguments. On Lunch Hour Legal Marketing, Filevine product director Josh Hostilo pitches the free client portal as real-time, saying every time the client touches the page it shows the most up-to-date information, an edge they claim over Case Status and Hona's nightly sync [9AejH9lLg90 @ 00:08:38]. Conrad Saam pushes back on the same panel that the walled garden is a limiting factor and that a forcing function can become problematic [9AejH9lLg90 @ 00:42:26]. Staffing splits too. Hostilo says to hire a dedicated platform admin rather than leaning on attorneys or paralegals, drawing on a prior 97-person firm, and steers small firms toward managed-service consultants. Vineskills sells exactly that alternative: hourly and optimization blocks billed month-to-month, so a firm is never locked into an extended engagement [9_hNat-thXA @ 00:39:59]. Sagar Pratap Singh, who spent 14-plus years selling outsourced paralegal support to US firms, argues from the small-firm side that nobody owns software buying, so the first move is naming an internal owner for the switch, tracking inquiry reply speed and weekly billed time for 90 days, and asking exactly how the data gets back out [mCa47xGWbys @ 00:12:49].

sections.title: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive failures are silent ones. Errol Janusz, who runs IT and cybersecurity for law offices, shows that reassigning a completed Filevine task to another user transfers it but leaves it invisible on the new user's task list; the demo reassignment to Ivan stayed complete and never surfaced, so the fix is a fresh thread through the write-a-note field rather than subtasks hung on the old task [mfKVI7JPrYc @ 00:01:16]. Stephanie at Vineskills names malpractice as the explicit risk: ask what happens if an automation fails against a deadline, avoid on-save and activity triggers that burn tasks, and lock trigger conditions to a test project ID while excluding the API user, because a loose trigger means that where you expected one item you have ten thousand [YtXAzduQ3PE @ 00:29:36]. Without an error recipe the system spams the admin inbox, a 504 timeout means a rerun, and too often teams set it and forget it because it worked once [YtXAzduQ3PE @ 00:51:21]. David at Vineskills adds that one trigger with a few actions is fair DIY territory, but bulk creates or deletes in a live environment are dangerous, with Zapier's replayable run history as the debugging lifeline [oNoHY7832hw @ 00:20:13].

Task metering is where the economics bite. David prices the Zapier Professional plan at roughly $30 a month on monthly billing for 750 tasks, warns the free plan likely cannot use the Filevine connector, and estimates three to five tasks per automation, so a two-to-three-task case-numbering build covers about 250 cases a month [oNoHY7832hw @ 00:32:24]. Mass tort volume changes the bill: clients near a million tasks or more run about $3,300 a month, loops are costly, and code blocks cut task use [oNoHY7832hw @ 00:31:30]. Trust math fails closed on purpose. In the LawAccounting demo, every fee code must total 100 percent, so trimming one line leaves 95 percent allocated and blocks progress, and cutting one settlement allocation from 175 to 170 on a $2M IOLTA wire left $500 unallocated before 12 receipts could post [dqv7XkRgaQQ @ 00:09:02]. On the time side, SelectHub's sponsored review, which credits Strong & Hanni with escaping $6,000 to $8,000 a month in storage overages, prices search friction at $66 lost per 10 minutes for a $400-an-hour attorney, and concedes Filevine may not suit solo practitioners with very low case volume or teams unwilling to invest in proper implementation [BBsBjTLqlDI @ 00:06:02].

Document handling carries irreversible traps. Libby at Vineskills, a former PI litigation paralegal, warns that redaction is permanent once saved, so copy the original first and hit the hidden save button; Bates stamping does not combine documents, so combine first, then stamp; share links require an expiration date, and deleting one erases its audit record [XAU9uhQg6nk @ 00:13:36]. Related-project note copying skips documents, document locks only release after about 24 hours, and a hundred tags buries the ten vitals the screen shows. Jay Stephanie of Levinson and Stefani, five years into Filevine, reports AI Fields still duplicating CPT codes while improving on ICD-10, so the firm orders records in three-month batches and deletes superfluous pages before upload, with a couple hundred pages taking five to ten minutes [TrEm-Mk2jeQ @ 00:15:30]. Susie Lewis flags that two date-of-accident fields of the native incident-date type auto-mirror and reject differing dates, and that automations cannot create UI features or popups [9_hNat-thXA @ 00:11:32]. On client messaging, Hostilo's rule is blunt: auto-text web leads a five-minute reply promise with the calling number, but never auto-reply to injury photos, and use keyword stops [9AejH9lLg90 @ 00:15:28].

chapters.question_prompt: How do firms obtain medical records cheaply under HITECH, review them at scale, and clear liens to get settlements paid?
chapters.title: HITECH Record Retrieval, AI Review & Settlement Administration
chapters.subtitle: HITECH Act and HIPAA changes, low-cost electronic record requests, retrieval challenges, AI chart review with Supio and Pattern Data, QSF operations, lien resolution, and the processes that delay payouts
chapters.executive_summary: Records lawyers, retrieval vendors, AI founders and settlement administrators converge on one thesis: mass tort is a volume game won by whoever controls medical records and structured data. The New York Injury & Malpractice Law Firm demands digital copies under HITECH, citing a $6.50 federal cap against $0.75-per-page paper billing, and targets 24-hour turnaround through records custodians. Pattern Data's Matt Francis reports 7 to 10x review throughput from litigation-specific AI lenses, while Tor Herman Law runs Supio across a 43,000-page NICU chart and 86 depositions. Archer's Gary Goldberg reports 90% of funds cleared in 10 to 14 months, with VA liens as the long poles, and LitPros claims 99% average lien reductions. The fault lines: who may sign a HITECH request, how far to trust OCR and AI, and whether open AI tools leak client health data.

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator on this beat starts from the same premise: mass tort is a volume business, and the medical record is the raw material. Bernadette Catalana, defense-side national coordinating counsel at MGM, puts the math bluntly: a typical lawyer carries 20 to 40 cases, while a mass tort lawyer may carry about 4,000, and organization is the only counter to that load, because missing a deadline or disclosure day is the risk [n2icO1gMkN8 @ 00:02:07]. Cara Wall watched the HRT litigation run to roughly 14,000 to 15,000 plaintiffs and reports current MDLs reaching hundreds of thousands [1O2RKMH06LU @ 00:06:30]. Inside those inventories, Supio CEO Jerry Joe estimates that 70 to 80 percent of all personal injury data is medical, which is why the platform ties that medical data into a knowledge graph [Yq68SC86WTQ @ 00:09:49]. Pattern Data founder Matt Francis frames the same reality as an infrastructure problem: mass tort requires structured data at scale, and the firms still stitching intake, outsourced review, CRMs and spreadsheets together by hand are paying for every data point and skipping re-evaluation because of it [_HuCGlH6Wyw @ 00:23:43]. The shared baseline is simple: control the records pipeline, structure what comes out of it, and the rest of the docket becomes manageable.

The second point of consensus is that HITECH is a retrieval weapon, not administrative paperwork. The New York Injury & Malpractice Law Firm tells every client to request records in digital form, because the 2009 law hands the patient the choice of format and caps the federal fee for digital copies at $6.50 regardless of page volume, while New York paper copies at up to 75 cents a page turn a 3,000 to 5,000 page file into a bill in the thousands [uJITvDxd4jA @ 00:00:39]. Bernard Nomberg in Birmingham reaches the same number from the preemption angle: federal law overrides state per-page schedules for electronic records, leaving $6.50 or a reasonable cost-based fee covering the labor to make the CD plus postage [_9ZPWIgPW14 @ 00:01:14]. The lawofmedicine breakdown of the HHS OCR rule confirms the access right sits on a reasonable fee for copy labor, and that business associates are now directly bound by HIPAA [n3wWlYBSpfg @ 00:02:00]. The New York firm's second video puts the spread in real dollars: about $6.50 for a CD holding 2,000 pages, versus roughly $1,500 at 75 cents a page and months of waiting [JdDeicrkI-o @ 00:00:23]. Nomberg adds that scanned paper and stored records from non-electronic providers still carry a flat fee with no per-page charge, so paper billing is the trap to refuse up front.

The third agreement cuts across vendors, founders and trial lawyers: AI accelerates the record work, but a human signs off. CERIS operations VP James Contes argues that even a 5% error rate applied to billions of dollars in claims at payers like United or HCA is gigantic money, so trained staff double-check OCR output with multiple QC and back-end QA passes, since OCR that misses the H&P triggers a second request [Coka2u38__k @ 00:17:43]. Matt Francis, whose entire company is AI-first, still says human expertise is critical and routes low-confidence calls such as pathology to experts while medical and smoking history come back near 100% confident [_HuCGlH6Wyw @ 00:19:24]. Tyler Schneider at Tor Herman Law runs Supio on trial work, yet warns to fact-check everything because blurred records and handwriting can fail OCR, and the firm's science lead Chad still reads every page [Yq68SC86WTQ @ 00:20:26]. Cara Wall uses AI for the first cut of medical chronologies and then puts humans on review, and treats any tool like a paralegal or associate [1O2RKMH06LU @ 00:19:43]. The baseline prerequisite all four share is a human validation layer between machine extraction and anything that reaches a matrix, a special master, or a jury.

sections.heading: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The retrieval playbook from The New York Injury & Malpractice Law Firm runs on speed, not patience. Portals are fast but incomplete, and the statutory 30-day deadline is almost always ignored, so the firm calls the records custodian directly, cites ongoing medical care, and asks for email delivery or sends a courier at a set time, chasing a 24-hour turnaround with follow-up calls [uJITvDxd4jA @ 00:01:48]. When a provider stonewalls with a $5,000 quote, the move is to narrow the request to the operative or imaging report, roughly 10 to 20 pages instead of 2,000 to 3,000, and if that fails, subpoena the records, since ignoring a subpoena means contempt; the firm has sued just to get records [uJITvDxd4jA @ 00:03:40]. The firm's no-expense routine adds a three-page cover letter citing HITECH that refuses to pay for paper, then a walk-in at Albany Medical Center with a HIPAA power of attorney to pick up a CD the next day, often at no charge, and a $10 Starbucks gift card, then scans the file into case-management software and burns CDs for experts [JdDeicrkI-o @ 00:02:35]. Bernard Nomberg flags one carve-out: X-ray films can carry a charge, so get a quote first because a third-party vendor may be involved [_9ZPWIgPW14 @ 00:03:36].

On the review side, Matt Francis builds one lens per litigation at Pattern Data and runs three products off it: same-day screening on usage, exposure timelines, diagnosis and evidentiary weight; development work on treatment patterns, severity, risk factors and gaps; and settlement packaging with eligibility, points or matrix valuation, and proof packets for a neutral or claims administrator [_HuCGlH6Wyw @ 00:06:16]. Valuation turns on dosage, duration, latency and cancer-subtype dividing lines, and Francis reliably sees 7 to 10x better throughput on case review, which matters when settlements land with 60, 90 or 120-day windows for thousands of clients [_HuCGlH6Wyw @ 00:13:03]. At Tor Herman Law, a NICU child's file ran 43,000 pages, where even a nurse summary at 10% would still be 4,300 pages; Supio filters by doctor or system and pulls weights and PT notes in real time, and across 86 depositions at seven hours each, or 602 hours, it surfaces contradictions from a witness deposed seven times, plus rebuttals to comparative-fault and preemption defenses [Yq68SC86WTQ @ 00:27:29]. Cara Wall's firm runs an over-20,000-case voluntary census by scraping medical records, then has humans spot-check, and answers show-cause attacks with percentages for proof of use and product ID [1O2RKMH06LU @ 00:18:04].

Downstream, the numbers come from administrators. Archer's Gary Goldberg says the term sheet or MOU stage takes several months before the MSA is final, a special master then needs a few additional months to build the matrix, and lien resolution has to clear Medicare, 50 state Medicaid agencies, health plans and military plans, with holdback payments arriving about 6 to 9 months post-allocation. Goldberg's benchmark is that 90% of funds are generally cleared and distributed within 10 to 14 months, with VA liens as the long poles [8CBO3CgHLvA @ 00:22:02]. Michelle Prince reports LitPros has worked thousands of Boy Scouts bankruptcy cases for about a year, cutting liens by 99% on average, around $72,000, after firms opted out of the trustee's vendor, and promises a 24-hour response on every email and call [73xfuxsKsEM @ 00:15:34]. On disbursement, Paige Richardson prices Milestone's Pathway at $200 per claimant, with Zelle, PayPal, ACH, paper check, or a custom prepaid Mastercard so unbanked claimants avoid check-casher fees [Y7FbfNp9_X4 @ 00:38:20]. Michael McCready, whose clients mostly complain about not hearing from the lawyer, sends seven to eight texts over 30 days after the release is mailed to the adjuster, at day 7, 10, 12, 14 and 21 [Y7FbfNp9_X4 @ 00:05:14].

sections.heading: 3. Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Record-access operators split on who pulls the trigger on a HITECH request and through which door. Bernard Nomberg of The Nomberg Law Firm teaches that the request has to be written by the patient, not the attorney, with the patient directing delivery to the lawyer, and that electronic copies carry no per-page fee, only $6.50 or a reasonable cost-based fee covering the labor to make the CD plus postage [_9ZPWIgPW14 @ 00:04:16]. The New York Injury & Malpractice Law Firm runs the opposite play: after a DC federal lower court barred lawyer requests, lawyers could again request digital records as of April 17, 2020, so the firm sends a three-page cover letter citing HITECH, refuses to pay for paper, and walks into Albany Medical Center with a HIPAA power of attorney to collect a CD the next day [JdDeicrkI-o @ 00:01:56]. The same firm writes off patient portals as fast but incomplete and 'not reliable at all,' preferring to call the records custodian, cite ongoing medical care, and push for a 24-hour turnaround [uJITvDxd4jA @ 00:01:15]. Jeannie Hennem of ChartFast, speaking on the CERIS Health panel, is betting the other way, forecasting Amazon-style e-commerce shopping for records riding on interoperability [Coka2u38__k @ 00:15:16].

The sharpest split among operators is how far to trust machine review. Matt Francis of Pattern Data claims 7 to 10x better throughput on case review and says medical and smoking history come back near 100% confident, with confidence grading routing only edge cases such as pathology to human experts [_HuCGlH6Wyw @ 00:13:03]. James Contes of CERIS Health counters that a 5% error rate on billions at United and HCA scale is 'gigantic dollars,' and that OCR missing the H&P triggers a second request, so trained staff double-check through multiple QC and back-end QA steps [Coka2u38__k @ 00:17:43]. Tyler Schneider of Tor Herman Law sits in the middle: Supio filters a 43,000-page NICU record by doctor or system in real time, yet the firm's science lead Chad still reads every page, and the LawNext line is blunt: 'you still have to be a lawyer' [Yq68SC86WTQ @ 00:31:22]. Cara Wall lets AI produce only the first cut of medical chronologies before human review, runs an over-20,000-case voluntary census by scraping records with human spot-checks, and treats Lexis AI strictly as a 'hunting tool' after a Stanford study showed a lower hallucination rate than Westlaw [1O2RKMH06LU @ 00:19:43].

On the back end, the timeline fight is stark. Gary Goldberg of Archer says 90% of funds are generally cleared and distributed within 10 to 14 months, with holdbacks landing about 6 to 9 months post-allocation and programs able to run first-in-first-out [8CBO3CgHLvA @ 00:22:02]. Paige Richardson of Milestone frames the claimant's reality as 5-plus years to settle and another 2 to distribute, and prices Pathway at $200 per claimant, 'well below the market standard,' with Zelle, PayPal, ACH, paper check or a prepaid Mastercard for unbanked claimants [Y7FbfNp9_X4 @ 00:20:00]. Lien playbooks diverge too: Michelle Prince of LitPros says raising liens at intake is a turn-off, yet pushes collecting health insurance information early and accurately, and pitches single-event lien work only to high-volume, tech-forward firms that integrate [73xfuxsKsEM @ 00:19:34]. On the vendor market, Francis calls the last 12 to 18 months of demand-letter and individual-tort entrants a 'bubble,' while host Gordon answers that competition is good [_HuCGlH6Wyw @ 00:24:25]. Francis insists Pattern is not document review, a general LLM summary or a chronology tool but cross-document inference, and predicts the platform integrating intake through claim forms wins.

sections.heading: 4. Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Record pulls bleed money and time at the request desk. The New York Injury & Malpractice Law Firm says the 30-day deadline is 'almost always' ignored and calls Syax and MRO charging 75 cents a page for digital records a 'total scam' that survives because nobody reports it; when stonewalled with a $5,000 quote, the fix is narrowing to the operative or imaging report, roughly 10 to 20 pages instead of 2,000 to 3,000 [uJITvDxd4jA @ 00:02:49]. The firm's own math: 2,000 pages in 24 hours on a CD, versus 75 cents a page, roughly $1,500, and months of waiting [JdDeicrkI-o @ 00:03:17]. On the vendor side, Jeannie Hennem of ChartFast reports a request sent to the wrong person sitting for weeks, 8 points of entry found in one case study, and SFTP deliveries corrupted by the vendor's own tech nearly triggering a takeback; lost requests mean lost revenue [Coka2u38__k @ 00:07:22]. Hennem also puts commingled patients from scanning errors in at least 2% of every project file, patched with NPIs plus OCR and actionable feedback to hospitals, while James Contes adds that systems switch ROI vendors unannounced and some centralize intake for 10 hospitals [Coka2u38__k @ 00:25:57].

The penalty history is the cautionary tale for any MSO or firm holding PHI in bulk. Dr. Peter Polack and Mike Meikle (Hawkthorne Group) walk through Cignet Health of Prince George's County, Maryland, which denied 41 patients their records between September 2008 and October 2009, stonewalled HHS, then delivered a truck full of thousands of records and ate a $4.3 million civil monetary penalty [CuDhCaHyZnI @ 00:01:51]. Two days later Mass General paid $1 million after an employee left documents on the subway containing PHI for 192 HIV/AIDS patients, never recovered, plus a corrective action plan and policy retooling that added cost. Their fix is process, not technology: train staff, encrypt storage, run asset management, know the laptop count, and enable remote wipe and tracking. lawofmedicine adds that HITECH binds business associates directly to HIPAA, so BA agreements need HIPAA and breach-notification language plus safeguards [n3wWlYBSpfg @ 00:03:04]. Michelle Prince of LitPros carries that into the AI era, warning that open AI tools leak legal and health data [73xfuxsKsEM @ 00:21:01], and Cara Wall's line is flat: don't upload client documents or sensitive things because they are not secure [1O2RKMH06LU @ 00:26:20].

Inventory and payout traps hit later and harder. Cara Wall warns that lawyers who bring in cases and don't work them hand the defense its meritless-case narrative, that PFS forms went from roughly a 15-page exercise to 60 to 80 pages, and that the Taxotere-style defense pulls social media for every plaintiff through show-cause and deficiency processes; dual representation means losing clients or sharing fees unless the firm keeps up client touches [1O2RKMH06LU @ 00:07:05]. Gary Goldberg of Archer cites a $100,000 lien sitting against a $30,000 settlement, probate and bankruptcy-trustee claims stacking delay, and VA liens as the long poles, noting it's not like going to one central source [8CBO3CgHLvA @ 00:19:06]. The Jon and Marc hosts add that bad reviews from waiting mass tort claimants hurt local PI SEO across a 3-to-10-year relationship, and Paige Richardson of Milestone reports Facebook claimant groups forming mini classes that generate bar complaints, while nine of ten callers just need information [Y7FbfNp9_X4 @ 00:13:51]. Matt Francis notes the old labor-only model made every data point a cost, so firms skipped re-evaluation even as criteria shifted mid-litigation [_HuCGlH6Wyw @ 00:04:40]. Bernadette Catalana pegs a mass tort load at about 4,000 cases, where a missed deadline or disclosure day is the risk.

callout.body: Every item below is a loss or near-miss practitioners hit firsthand; clear each one before pushing volume through the pipeline.

chapters.question_prompt: How does litigation finance work, and how do funders underwrite mass-tort and PI firms?
chapters.title: Litigation Finance Fundamentals for Mass-Tort Firms
chapters.subtitle: How funding works, when litigation finance met mass torts, underwriting criteria, plaintiff vs. defendant funding, benefits to law firms, class-action funding, funder risk and returns, and mass-tort funding hot topics
chapters.executive_summary: Mass-tort practitioners agree that funding has shifted from single-case bets to loan-like portfolio facilities lent to law firms, mostly to buy advertising and work up thousands of claims, with the funder paid from the lawyers' 20 to 40 percent fee rather than the plaintiff's share. Ted Farrell prices the workup at about $3,000 per case, or roughly $30 million for 10,000 clients; Bloomberg puts portfolio pricing around a 20 percent interest rate, and Rocade writes $10 million to $50 million facilities with a $10 million minimum. Funders say they take no control, select only 5 to 10 percent of deals, and underwrite by injury subtype because "Data is everything." Disagreement runs through the mechanics: Bloomberg's sources call mass-tort deals win-or-lose repayment loans, while commercial funders sell non-recourse ratchets of 2x to 3x and a 10x value-to-commitment rule.

key_metrics.value: Around a 20% interest rate
key_metrics.context: Typical return on loan-like portfolio funding spread across thousands of mass-tort cases, paid from the lawyers' slice rather than the plaintiff's.

key_metrics.value: $3,000 per case x 10,000 clients = about $30M
key_metrics.context: Ted Farrell's per-case workup math covering filing fees of $400-500, medical records orders, and nurse review across a large mass-tort docket.

key_metrics.context: Share of submitted deals that survive underwriting on merits, claim holder, and counsel, with funders offering about 10% of expected recovery.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Across Bloomberg's reporting and the advisers who structure the deals, the core consensus is that mass-tort money is not the old single-case bet. Bloomberg Television frames the shift plainly: single-case funding was the original model, but mass-tort funding is structured "more like a loan win or lose the investor gets paid," with portfolio funding that hedges risk across thousands of cases [dg6Bt8bmJmQ @ 00:05:24]. Ted Farrell, who founded Litigation Funding Advisors in 2019 after working both as a funding-user lawyer and as an MD at a global legal finance firm, confirms that mass-tort money is mostly loans to law firms, used heavily for advertising [gdDT2WSKYs0 @ 00:07:20]. That advertising spend is measurable: advertisers know how many calls each ad generates, and social media and AI play a growing role in intake [D9nqJXMXzRI @ 00:04:32]. The economic engine underneath is the contingency fee. Lawyers typically earn 20 to 40 percent of settlements or awards but are paid only at settlement or trial, which is the cash gap funders fill. On Camp Lejeune, Bloomberg notes the funder's cut comes out of the lawyers' slice, not the plaintiff's, so the firm, not the client, bears the cost of capital [D9nqJXMXzRI @ 00:06:36].

The second point of agreement is the risk transfer itself. Express Legal Funding calls it "the absolute key": the deal "is almost always non recourse," meaning a third party pays legal bills for a share of the win, and on a loss the funder gets nothing [AVBbpi6lPFY @ 00:01:03]. Dave Kirsty of Arcadia, who came up through Gibson Dunn, Bentham IMF and Validity, adds the control piece: "funders don't take any control over the matter," holding only a right to updates [fTOe5KR6QSE @ 00:04:31]. Casey Gard of GFO Asset Management, with 30-plus years in finance and roughly eight years in litigation finance, says the same from the funder chair: funders cannot dictate strategy, and half his team are legal professionals, including five lawyers [g66VtR5b5gQ @ 00:32:29]. The Oregon Law Lab frames the financial position simply: a funder acts like a contingency attorney financially, and established funders are not gambling because they back "more likely than not" winners [TyGsfcYU1dw @ 00:08:34]. For a mass-tort shop, that means outside money arrives without an outside voice on strategy, as long as the firm clears underwriting first. Gard's own summary of the arrangement is blunt: "It's balancing the playing field."

The third consensus is that funders say no far more often than yes, and the yes depends on data. TownCenter Partners ranks the underwriting criteria as merits first, then the claim holder, then counsel, and reports that only 5 to 10 percent of deals get selected, with funders wanting non-emotional claim holders who will settle and have skin in the game [5XWpCPDxugc @ 00:02:00]. The Oregon Law Lab's number is tighter still: funders take about 5 percent of cases or less, leaving a "huge unmet need" [TyGsfcYU1dw @ 00:05:59]. Adam Rosen, MD of Underwriting at Rocade and a former Ashcraft & Gerel MDL litigator, reduces the mass-tort version to three words: "Data is everything." He wants firms to plan data capture beyond intake, including fee splits, expenses and surgery dates, and to run quality control and SOPs [Zz1HlCrfQPY @ 00:30:27]. TownCenter pitches this selectivity as a benefit: funders' data analysis improves the firm's own case selection, funding increases demand for legal services on both plaintiff and defense sides, and it counters downward pressure on fees because funders have no reason to demand discounted hourly rates [yYpZT2DR1fE @ 00:01:04]. The baseline prerequisite is clean, granular docket data.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Start with the cash-burn math, because that is what the loan actually pays for. Farrell itemizes the hard costs per mass-tort case: $400 to $500 in filing fees, medical records orders and nurse review, with full case workup running "thousands" per case [gdDT2WSKYs0 @ 00:08:27]. Scale it and the number gets ugly fast: at $3,000 per case, 10,000 clients means about $30 million, and Farrell paraphrases the casual pitch of "at 3,000 bucks a pop you know just come up with 15 million bucks and you too could you know be doing those cases" [gdDT2WSKYs0 @ 00:10:38]. Camp Lejeune adds a layer, since those claims require an individual administrative process before filing. Gard runs the same arithmetic from the funder side: 500 cases at $10,000 each is $5 million laid out before any money comes back [g66VtR5b5gQ @ 00:22:25]. Rocade's ticket sizes reflect that scale. Rosen describes the core product as bank-like law-firm debt, with facilities typically running $10 million to $50 million, a $10 million minimum, and some deals above $100 million, under a "low volume, high quality" posture [Zz1HlCrfQPY @ 00:07:26]. Firms that show up ready close in four to six weeks; messy firms take months. Farrell's own matchmaking range spans $2 million single cases up to $50 million whole-firm loans.

Pricing splits by structure. On mass-tort portfolio loans, Bloomberg reports returns usually around a 20 percent interest rate [D9nqJXMXzRI @ 00:06:01]. Single-case and commercial deals price off ratchets instead. Kirsty lays out a typical ladder: 2x or 15 percent at one year, 2.5x or 20 percent at two years, and 3x or 25 percent at three years, with an alternative structure of 2x plus 10 percent; the target is for the client to keep 50 to 60 percent or more of the recovery [fTOe5KR6QSE @ 00:10:00]. His worked example: a $10 million budget against a $100 million expected resolution, the client puts in $100,000, the funder takes 3x or $30 million, the firm takes 20 percent or $20 million, and the client keeps $50 million, a "500x" return on its own outlay. That example was built to fit his 10x rule, where case value should run about 10 times the commitment and funders cap at 50 to 70 percent of the budget [fTOe5KR6QSE @ 00:12:59]. Farrell explains why docket structure cuts price: mature, diversified dockets with a track record price as credit-style deals, while single cases can go to "negative eight or negative ten" on summary judgment and even a trade-secret case carries about a 20 percent total-loss risk [gdDT2WSKYs0 @ 00:15:05].

Underwriting a mass-tort docket is granular work. Rosen values every case by injury subtype rather than a settlement average, and in 2020 Rocade modeled three separate 3M grids [Zz1HlCrfQPY @ 00:28:47]. On the buy side, Farrell says a $20 million non-recourse loan against a docket likely returns 40, 60, 80 or 100, calls the asset uncorrelated with markets, and describes the money going in as "very smart" [gdDT2WSKYs0 @ 00:12:37]. James Koutoulas, who runs the Typhon hedge fund and recovered about $7 billion for 48,000 accounts in MF Global and PFG, is building liquidity for that buyer pool through Juris Trade, a secondary market and securitization platform. His PCP bond pays insured principal plus 12 percent simple interest, with a preferred tranche reaching up to 20 percent IRR, and he splits buyers into MOIC investors chasing 2x to 40x and IRR investors [4PHHiyG2S5k @ 00:21:32]. Express Legal Funding's commercial example shows how tiered returns land at exit: a funder commits $3 million to a patent case running four years with appeals, the return climbs to the top 4x tier, and a $25 million settlement pays the funder $12 million while the company keeps $13 million [AVBbpi6lPFY @ 00:03:22].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Control over the case is the sharpest split among the operators. Dave Kirsty of Arcadia, a Gibson Dunn and Bentham IMF veteran, states flatly that “funders don't take any control over the matter,” with the funder holding only a right to updates [fTOe5KR6QSE @ 00:04:31]. Casey Gard of GFO Asset Management backs that line from the mass-tort side, saying funders cannot dictate strategy and pointing out that half of the GFO team are legal professionals, including five lawyers [g66VtR5b5gQ @ 00:32:29]. Express Legal Funding draws a different map: commercial deals worth millions in patent and antitrust cases are where the funder may have a say in strategy, and the cons list explicitly includes possible funder input on settlement decisions alongside complex contracts and disclosure demands [AVBbpi6lPFY @ 00:05:26]. Bloomberg Law frames the same fight as an open market controversy, reporting critics who fear funder control over settlement while funders deny it, and predicting that disclosure regulation is coming to an industry still described as the Wild West [z3Bd4lWO460 @ 00:03:22]. Operators therefore face contradictory testimony on the default: non-recourse capital with zero control on one side, and strategy and settlement input written into commercial contracts on the other.

The second fault line is whether funding manufactures cases. Bloomberg Law reports critics who say mass-tort money leads firms to file claims “without Merit,” set against a market where lawyers collect 20 to 40 percent and MDLs typically settle “sometimes without much judicial oversight” [D9nqJXMXzRI @ 00:07:15]. Bloomberg Television carries the same critique in sharper form, with opponents arguing the capital fuels “unnecessary cases… without a clear injury” while advertisers track exactly how many calls each ad generates [dg6Bt8bmJmQ @ 00:07:15]. Casey Gard answers from the funder chair with a blunt counter: “It has not created a single claim,” framing the money as a way of balancing the playing field, echoing the same panel's point that insurers have always funded the defense [g66VtR5b5gQ @ 00:26:09]. Stephen O'Dowd of Harbour goes further and dismisses the “alarmists” who forecast an explosion of claims, pointing to loser-pays costs as a natural check and noting that in the UK “not a single claim has been certified, which I think is quite telling” after four years of the competition-only regime [22mFLcrQrE8 @ 00:03:58]. O'Dowd's forecast is “measured growth,” while the Bloomberg critics treat MDL consolidation itself as the engine that raises settlements, funds the next wave of cases, and pulls in outside investors.

Structure is the third split, and it changes who eats the loss. Bloomberg Law defines litigation finance as a bet where a losing case leaves the funder “out all their money” [z3Bd4lWO460 @ 00:00:39], but Bloomberg Television reports that mass-tort money has moved to loan-like portfolio funding hedged across thousands of cases, where “win or lose the investor gets paid,” usually at around a 20 percent interest rate [dg6Bt8bmJmQ @ 00:05:24]. Ted Farrell of Litigation Funding Advisors prices the same gap from the buy side: mature, diversified dockets with a track record trade as credit-style deals, while single cases can go to “negative eight or negative ten” on summary judgment and firm loans rarely lose everything [gdDT2WSKYs0 @ 00:15:40]. James Koutoulas of Juris Trade splits the capital itself into two camps, MOIC investors hunting 2x to 40x outcomes versus IRR investors, and builds a PCP bond with insured principal plus 12 percent simple interest and a preferred tranche reaching up to 20 percent IRR for the yield crowd [4PHHiyG2S5k @ 00:31:16]. Single-case commercial deals run on ratchets and multiples; mass-tort dockets run on loan math. Firms choosing a playbook are choosing which investor profile sits across the table.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The first trap is the cash hole that opens before a single dollar comes back. Casey Gard walks through the arithmetic: 500 cases at $10,000 each means $5 million laid out up front, and Dodd-Frank-era limits keep banks from lending against contingency assets, which is why firms land at funders' doors [g66VtR5b5gQ @ 00:22:25]. Ted Farrell itemizes the hard costs behind that number, with $400 to $500 filing fees, medical record orders, and nurse review pushing workup into the thousands per case, so that 10,000 clients at $3,000 each becomes roughly $30 million [gdDT2WSKYs0 @ 00:10:38]. Farrell mocks the advertising pitch directly: “at 3,000 bucks a pop you know just come up with 15 million bucks and you too could you know be doing those cases” [gdDT2WSKYs0 @ 00:09:21]. Dave Kirsty names the two internal gaps that turn that burn into a crisis: poor budgeting and no partner-compensation mechanism for cases carried on risk, a problem that bites because funders cap their commitment at 50 to 70 percent of the budget [fTOe5KR6QSE @ 00:14:45]. Camp Lejeune adds a timing drag on top, since every claim requires an individual administrative process before filing, stretching the period in which cash is out and nothing is returning.

Valuation errors are the second recurring loss. Adam Rosen of Rocade, an ex-Ashcraft & Gerel MDL litigator, warns that naive per-plaintiff averaging overvalues “product in place” dockets, and the firms that lean on it keep refinancing instead of getting paid [Zz1HlCrfQPY @ 00:52:13]. Rocade's fix is to value every case by injury subtype rather than a settlement average, which is how the shop modeled three separate 3M grids in 2020, and Rosen's blunt summary is “Data is everything,” meaning fee splits, expenses and surgery dates tracked well beyond intake [Zz1HlCrfQPY @ 00:28:47]. TownCenter Partners breaks personal-injury value into damages, liability and insurance, noting that damages only come clear after maximum medical improvement and that liability is the hardest piece to calculate [1Xs5nnkcuL4 @ 00:01:35]. Dave Kirsty adds the final check: winning is not the same as collecting, and firms must build their case math around collectability, with case value sitting at roughly 10x the commitment so the waterfall still works after the funder's multiple [fTOe5KR6QSE @ 00:15:42]. A docket that looks rich on averages, unvalidated by subtype, MMI status and collection prospects, is the docket that ends in a refinancing loop rather than a payout.

The third category is counterparty and rule-change risk that firms rarely see coming. Ted Farrell warns that some funders are past their fund's investment period and will not admit it, which is why advisers time approaches for moments such as right after a “fund two” closes [gdDT2WSKYs0 @ 00:18:57]. Farrell also flags odd clauses buried in documents that have no standard form, including attorney-in-fact rights triggered on a “material risk of a bankruptcy” [gdDT2WSKYs0 @ 00:20:13]. Adam Rosen tells firms to hire transactional counsel and to raise capital only when reinvestment returns beat its cost, and saves the harshest warning for MSO deals: “You're trading away a ton of upsides for a little upfront cash,” with California cited as a regulatory wipeout risk for those structures [Zz1HlCrfQPY @ 01:24:31]. Rosen also notes that North Carolina's ban blocks some appeal deals outright, so jurisdiction decides which products are even available. Oregon Law Lab adds that a change in law or treaty mid-case can make an investment worthless “or even negative,” the flip side of the hedge-fund pitch that litigation holds value whether the market goes up or down [TyGsfcYU1dw @ 00:04:45].

callout.title: Four Gates Before Taking Docket Capital
callout.body: Every gate below comes from a loss, a refinancing loop, or a contract trap that a named practitioner reported firsthand. Clear all four before signing a facility.
items: Run the full per-case workup cost first: at $3,000 per case, 10,000 clients is roughly $30 million, so size the facility to the real burn, not the advertising pitch [Slarskey LLC — gdDT2WSKYs0 @ 00:10:38].

Kill per-plaintiff averaging: value the docket by injury subtype and have fee splits, expenses and surgery dates captured beyond intake with QC and SOPs in place [The Heart of Law Podcast — Zz1HlCrfQPY @ 00:29:48].
Confirm the funder is still inside its fund's investment period and strip odd clauses such as attorney-in-fact rights on a material risk of a bankruptcy [Slarskey LLC — gdDT2WSKYs0 @ 00:20:13].
Raise capital only when reinvestment returns exceed its cost, and bring transactional counsel to the table before term sheets turn into contracts [The Heart of Law Podcast — Zz1HlCrfQPY @ 00:49:04].

action_checklist: Size every funding ask against the 10x rule: a $10 million commitment should sit against roughly a $100 million expected resolution [ResTech Solutions — fTOe5KR6QSE @ 00:13:12].
Build the data stack before the raise: fee splits, expenses and surgery dates tracked beyond intake, backed by QC and written SOPs [The Heart of Law Podcast — Zz1HlCrfQPY @ 00:29:48].
Time the approach to funders for windows such as right after a fund two closes, when fresh capital needs deploying [Slarskey LLC — gdDT2WSKYs0 @ 00:19:28].
Negotiate the return ratchet (2x/15% at year one up to 3x/25% at year three, or 2x plus 10%) so the client keeps 50 to 60 percent or more [ResTech Solutions — fTOe5KR6QSE @ 00:11:17].
Package the firm cleanly so the facility closes in 4 to 6 weeks instead of dragging for months like messy firms [The Heart of Law Podcast — Zz1HlCrfQPY @ 00:37:06].

Pre-screen each case on the funder's three underwriting criteria, merits first, then claim holder and counsel, since only 5 to 10 percent of deals get selected [TownCenter Partners Litigation Finance — 5XWpCPDxugc @ 00:00:30].

chapters.question_prompt: How are investors and private equity treating lawsuits and law firms as assets, and what deal structures result?
chapters.title: Capital Markets Meet the Law Firm: Portfolio Funding, PE & Law-Firm MSOs
chapters.subtitle: Litigation as an asset class, funding market process, portfolio and law-firm financing, investor perspectives, ethics of non-lawyer capital, PE consolidation, and MSOs for contingency-fee firms
chapters.executive_summary: Holland & Knight's Trisha Rich and Josh Port, Lucian Pera, Tim Mackey and the Esquire Bank panel converge on one blueprint. Spin non-lawyer staff, equipment, IP and founder likeness into a Delaware LLC MSO. Lease it back for a fixed monthly or cost-plus fee, with 10-15% markups, validated by a third-party fairness opinion. Keep lawyers, engagement letters, trust accounts, hiring, case selection and settlement inside the firm. Accounting trades near 15x EBITDA versus 4-8x for law firms, and Joe Prencipe pitches buying in at 5x to roll up PI firms running 35% margins. On the funding side, Burford funds 6-8% of reviewed cases at mid-20s IRRs, and 39 funders committed $2.8B in 2025. Disagreements center on mass-tort cash-flow unpredictability, the timing of Am Law deals, securitization, and whether portfolio deals are truly diversified.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Holland & Knight's Trisha Rich frames the MSO bluntly: it is 'simply a vendor,' and nobody is buying law firms [5TjsKzLtyc4 @ 00:03:09]. Every practitioner describing the build lands on the same split. Tim Mackey of Vista Consulting spins all non-lawyer staff, leases and the licensed brand out of the law firm into the managed service organization, which leases them back while the firm makes a lease payment [lgURVgZL9IY @ 00:01:14]. On Mattern LLC, Holland & Knight's Josh and Trish add equipment, IP and the founders' name, image and likeness to the transfer list, while lawyers, engagement letters and trust accounts stay inside the firm [8wwcTCIWOXM @ 00:05:26]. HR and accounting can migrate to the management company; hiring and firing, case selection and settlement authority never do. On The LegalTech Fund, Rich calls the vehicle a 'two company model' or LSO, a parallel management company that handles administrative and business functions and that anyone, including non-lawyers, can own, provided it never owns or controls the lawyers and is never paid in a way that amounts to a fee split [kF2XWwBObZ8 @ 00:04:08]. The operator takeaway is consistent across these speakers: the investor buys the business chassis, never the practice, and every dollar of value has to be engineered on that boundary.

The second consensus point is payment. Rich is categorical that no percentage of profits or revenue is allowed: the fee must be a fixed monthly number or cost-plus, backed by a third-party fairness opinion [5TjsKzLtyc4 @ 00:23:21]. The Esquire Bank panel with Chad Dudley and Tim Mackey describes the same discipline, with the valuation done by outside professionals and 'not tied to the revenue of the law firm,' run through licensing agreements or cost-plus arrangements [epFmlanyChw @ 00:01:28]. Lucian Pera of Adams and Reese says MSOs are legal and, structured correctly, trigger no Rule 5.4 problem, even though ethics opinions are the thinnest precedent and Texas only blesses the pieces rather than the whole [wXttJe-HCVM @ 00:05:40]. Rich dismisses the common owner fear of 'anybody coming in here and telling me what to do' as 'a little bit overblown,' because the two ethical pillars, no control and no fee-splitting, wall the investor off from the lawyering [kF2XWwBObZ8 @ 00:10:08]. Every state except Arizona carries a version of Rule 5.4, and the concern is control as well as ownership, so the fee mechanism and the control map are where every deal is judged. The Mattern walkthrough adds that regulators elevate 'substance over form,' so a cost-plus label will not rescue a fee that behaves like a revenue share.

The third consensus thread is that outside capital only works with a plan attached. Pera calls the MSO 'a tool... not for everyone,' rejects 'management by inflight magazine,' and insists the business plan comes first, citing an AI tool for construction clients as the example, and says a bank or 'uncle Jim' may be easier [wXttJe-HCVM @ 00:07:22]. Rich runs the same fit test from the deal desk: if the capital would just sit in savings, an MSO 'might not be for you' [kF2XWwBObZ8 @ 00:08:10]. On the litigation-finance side of the capital stack, the funders agree on the terms that make the money palatable. GLS Capital's Hannah Sadler explains that funding is non-recourse, so if the case is lost or dismissed 'the litigant doesn't owe anything to the funder,' and that funders do not control the litigation [9teRv9eFpEc @ 00:05:13]. Bentham's Dave Kirstine says the only rights retained after investing are to be kept informed, to weigh in on settlement and to be paid, and Drumcliff's Jim Little and Michael Weiss likewise exercise no control [rQPZlRgHcfE @ 00:56:12]. Whether the money arrives as MSO equity or case funding, the common denominator is passive capital backing a firm that keeps running its own cases.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The Mattern LLC walkthrough gives the build order. Step one is forming the MSO, 'typically just a Delaware LLC' [8wwcTCIWOXM @ 00:04:03]. Non-legal assets then move across, and the MSO licenses or leases them back under a business services agreement for a monthly fee, with an accounting firm validating fairness; the stated goal is to move as much economics as is defensible, net of attorney compensation [8wwcTCIWOXM @ 00:06:30]. Only then does the investor buy all or part of the MSO, either for partner liquidity or growth capital. Valuation is built vertical by vertical, marketing, HR and so on, and the rules do not require fair market value; it functions as a defense. On fee levels, Rich puts typical cost-plus markups at 10-15%, and says fee changes should be forward-looking only, with the fairness analysis refreshed; an annual cadence 'seems more or less sensible,' though there are no hard and fast rules [5TjsKzLtyc4 @ 00:25:36]. The Esquire Bank panel structures the agreement by defining the services, the MSO-owned IP and the resources used, then paying a fixed monthly amount like any vendor, re-evaluated as MSO headcount grows, usually yearly and sometimes sooner [epFmlanyChw @ 00:01:08]. Annual re-pricing is the shared default across both camps.

Because lawyers cannot be bound by non-competes, even in an asset sale, and Josh Port warns there are 'no silver bullets,' the deal paper has to do the retention work. The Mattern walkthrough lists the levers: rollover equity, equity forfeiture, and five-year vesting of cash, for example returning 60% if a lawyer quits in year two [8wwcTCIWOXM @ 00:19:20]. Name, image and likeness licenses are another lever, and the Jon and Marc panel reports these run 'in perpetuity' and can permit AI versions of the founder [U2xFBBUm_IU @ 00:20:06]. Rich flags two drafting traps that show up in investor paper. First, personal liability for unpaid MSO fees should be rewritten as deferred fees [5TjsKzLtyc4 @ 00:42:21]. Second, non-solicitation covenants that reach lawyers or clients violate Rule 5.6 and have to come out. Plans cut both ways: an investor that arrives without a performance plan is a 'yellow flag,' and a firm that takes money without its own plan faces 'a tremendous amount of pressure' from equity partners to pay it out in compensation [8wwcTCIWOXM @ 00:42:49]. On the exit side, the Jon and Marc panelists say less founder reliance earns a higher EBITDA multiple and that a couple of years of track record matters.

Litigation funding has its own mechanics on the same capital map. Bentham's Dave Kirstine sets a $1-1.5M minimum with a $5-15M wheelhouse, wants case value at 8-10x the commitment, and runs intake, NDA, an in-person meeting, a non-binding term sheet within about a week, then binding 30-45 day exclusivity [rQPZlRgHcfE @ 00:11:07]. Much Shelist's Jonathan Friedland lays out the formal market process: rifled rather than shotgun outreach, an anonymized teaser, CA, CIM, term sheet, diligence, then the funding agreement [9teRv9eFpEc @ 00:26:04]. Selectivity is brutal: Hannah Sadler reports about 4 funded per hundreds reviewed, and Statera's Stewart Ackerly prices on a multiple of capital actually drawn, often less than the commitment. Burford's Chris Bogart says Burford funds only 6-8% of the cases it reviews and describes the default waterfall: capital back first, then a time-based multiple starting around 0.5x and rising, then a share of net recovery; on $10 million deployed, Burford looks for '$10 million back and then another $5 million' on the time-based leg [1kAfGIkF10g @ 00:27:53]. Bogart reports mid-20s IRRs, ROIC in the 80s and a per-case loss rate under 10%, with appeal-stage SDNY cases priced cheap and multi-jurisdiction arbitrations priced expensive.

sections.heading: 3. Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is over what an investor actually buys. Trisha Rich of Holland & Knight calls an MSO 'simply a vendor' and says nobody is buying law firms; the MSO cannot hire or fire lawyers, set settlement parameters, or control client intake [5TjsKzLtyc4 @ 00:03:09]. Law firm owner Joe Prencipe pitches the same vehicle to PE, strategic acquirers, and family offices as the opportunity 'to buy all or part of a law firm,' backed by partners averaging $4M, PI niches running 35% margins, and a roll-up thesis of buying in at 5x EBITDA and expanding into nearby cities [R60PdSP1C24 @ 00:00:28]. The healthcare precedent splits the room too. Tim Mackey of Vista Consulting, sell-side advisor on the biggest public deal, warns that PE in medicine 15 to 20 years ago degraded service and that the fear is 'profits over plaintiffs,' while insisting lawyers retain all legal control and Vista will demand alignment [lgURVgZL9IY @ 00:11:11]. Rich answers that critics cite medical MSOs 'on purpose' as the worst case and that accounting, where deals trade around 15x EBITDA against 4 to 8x for law firms, is the honest analog [5TjsKzLtyc4 @ 00:09:49]. Same legal skeleton, two sales pitches: vendor contract on one side, ownership stake with a growth mandate on the other.

Capital providers split just as hard on whether to lend or to own. Alex Garnier of North Wall Capital wants downside protection: a loan to the law firm, debt repaid before any profit share, diversification, and near-settlement cases to offset duration, and warns that single-case funding tempts firms to run up costs [QpKDhqASBqM @ 00:03:31]. On securitization the same Brown Rudnick panel fractured: Garnier says yes eventually, at hundreds of millions minimum with North Wall taking the junior tranche, while Burford's Leo disagrees, citing disclosure, size, and the point that capital is not the problem [QpKDhqASBqM @ 00:56:17]. Josh Meltzer of Infinitive, who runs an IP Finance group, attacks the comfort of law-firm lending from another angle: PIK interest erodes LTV and over-collateralization every year until the loan is 'Equity like' [l-KmnCtiBMg @ 00:13:12]. David Perla, after about 8 years at Burford, goes further and says litigation finance already 'behaves like an equity investment,' and Burford takes minority, passive law-firm stakes with no mandate to sell and pitches itself as a permanent partner rather than a 3 to 6 year PE seller [CdJKmwCQvOw @ 00:25:26]. Lender, quasi-equity, or permanent partner: that is the real choice buried in the term sheet.

Nobody agrees on how far up-market this goes or who should bother. Lucian Pera calls an MSO 'a tool… not for everyone,' rejects 'management by inflight magazine,' demands a business plan first, and says a bank or 'uncle Jim' may be the easier money [wXttJe-HCVM @ 00:08:47]. Rich runs the same filter from the deal desk: if the capital would just sit in savings, an MSO 'might not be for you,' even though about two-thirds of the roughly 50 live deals on that Holland & Knight team are consumer-facing SSDI and plaintiff PI shops [kF2XWwBObZ8 @ 00:08:10]. On scale, the Jon and Marc panel predicts hourly and Am Law 100 MSOs, then hundreds of deals followed by thousands, and flags that an MSO exit sells a service provider while an ABS exit sells a law firm [U2xFBBUm_IU @ 00:39:41]. David Perla pushes back on the big-firm hype: boutiques are the early movers over 3 to 5 years, big checks need firms with 1 to 5 owners, there is no critical mass of Am Law 100/200 PE deals, and Perla rejects a podcast guest's call for 3 to 5 Am Law 200 equity deals in 2026 backed by sovereign wealth funds [CdJKmwCQvOw @ 00:47:06]. Pera reduces the ABS-versus-MSO fork to a single question: how much control do you want.

sections.heading: 4. Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The first trap is assuming the money locks the lawyers in place. Josh Port of Holland & Knight says lawyers cannot be bound by non-competes, even in an asset sale, the risk cannot be eliminated, and there are 'no silver bullets' [5TjsKzLtyc4 @ 00:06:46]. On the Mattern LLC session, the Holland & Knight workaround stack is rollover equity, equity forfeiture, and 5-year vesting of cash, with a lawyer who quits in year two returning 60%, plus name/image/likeness licenses that keep the founder's brand inside the MSO [8wwcTCIWOXM @ 00:19:20]. Rich's red-flag list for deal drafts catches the overreach: personal liability for unpaid MSO fees should be restructured as deferred fees, and non-solicitation covenants covering lawyers or clients violate Rule 5.6 [5TjsKzLtyc4 @ 00:42:21]. The fee itself is the second tripwire. No percentage of profits or revenue is allowed; fees must be fixed monthly or cost-plus, typically at 10 to 15% markups, backed by a third-party fairness opinion, and any change should be forward-looking with the fairness analysis refreshed [5TjsKzLtyc4 @ 00:23:21]. Rich says there are no hard and fast rules on cadence, but annual resets seem 'more or less sensible.' Each clause is where a sloppy draft breaks the ethics rules the whole structure leans on.

Control and cash discipline produce the war stories. The Jon and Marc panel points to the UnitedLex bankruptcy, where the court found the MSO exerted improper control, and insists majority and minority rights be contracted up front rather than improvised later [U2xFBBUm_IU @ 00:17:08]. On the Mattern LLC session, Holland & Knight warns that taking the money without a plan invites 'a tremendous amount of pressure' from equity partners to pay it out in compensation, and an investor arriving without a performance plan is a 'yellow flag' [8wwcTCIWOXM @ 00:39:23]. Mass torts carry their own cash-flow problem: the same Jon and Marc panel says the challenge for PE is 'the unpredictability of cash flow,' compounded by fund duration, so far only 'bucket B' deals, PI firms with systematic mass-tort programs, are getting done, with one closing within weeks [U2xFBBUm_IU @ 00:08:35]. Marketing economics can sink the roll-up thesis from below: the panel reports $300-per-click bidding pricing out small firms, cost per case rising, and almost no PI clients still running traditional Google Ads [U2xFBBUm_IU @ 00:38:11]. The squeeze runs both ways, because regional firms also face 'Death Star' capital as Morgan & Morgan and Sweet James enter markets, and the panel calls PE money 'an accelerant' for that pressure.

On the litigation finance side, the failures are pricing and duration errors. Judgment preservation insurance was born in 2021 and gone by 2023, mispriced because appellate risk runs about 50/50; 'So the product is now in my view gone,' says a National Law Review panelist, while Stewart Ackerly of Statera warns post-judgment collection is riskier than litigants assume [9teRv9eFpEc @ 01:01:19]. Josh Meltzer runs the IRR check: making two times your money over more than 10 years is 'less good on an irr basis' [l-KmnCtiBMg @ 00:09:32]. Chris Bogart of Burford flags low-but-positive outcomes, such as a $7M verdict or $11M settlement on a case expected to be worth $100M, as the problem case, and Burford's contracts carry worked payout examples at different outcome levels; Bogart also concedes $5M SME claims are effectively squeezed out [1kAfGIkF10g @ 00:55:54]. Sean Campbell of Valiant, selling 24-month notes at 15% per year secured at roughly 1.5x collateral against post-bellwether mass-tort fees, has not yet found a post-bellwether loss, but says that if one happens it is 'game over,' and investor statements simply rise 'a little over a percent' a month with no mark-to-market [FQLjhMdShl0 @ 00:24:22].

action_checklist: Map which assets move: non-lawyer staff, equipment, IP, and founder name/image/likeness go into a Delaware LLC MSO, while lawyers, engagement letters, and trust accounts stay in the firm [Mattern LLC — 8wwcTCIWOXM @ 00:05:26].
Commission an outside valuation, set a fixed monthly or cost-plus fee not tied to firm revenue, and re-evaluate it yearly or sooner as MSO headcount grows [Esquire Bank — epFmlanyChw @ 00:01:08].
Build the departure defense with rollover equity, equity forfeiture, and 5-year cash vesting before the investor wires money [Mattern LLC — 8wwcTCIWOXM @ 00:19:20].
Prep the exit by cutting founder reliance, logging a couple of years of track record, moving to cloud CMS, and setting key-person succession [Jon and Marc — U2xFBBUm_IU @ 00:21:38].
Run funder outreach as a rifle, not a shotgun: anonymized teaser, CA, CIM, term sheet, diligence, then funding agreement [The National Law Review — 9teRv9eFpEc @ 00:26:04].
Size the ask to the funder's floor: Bentham's minimum is $1 to 1.5M with a $5 to 15M wheelhouse and case value at 8 to 10x the commitment [OffshoreAlert — rQPZlRgHcfE @ 00:11:07].

chapters.question_prompt: How are MSOs and Arizona ABS structures set up, and what risks and traps come with them?
chapters.title: MSO & ABS Structures: Healthcare Models, Fee Traps & Arizona's Experiment
chapters.subtitle: Healthcare MSO basics and reasons to form one, California and Texas MSO models, law-firm MSO fee traps and advisor views, and Arizona ABS rules, updates, risks, and operator case studies
chapters.executive_summary: Healthcare and law-firm practitioners describe the same split: a licensed professional entity that owns the practice and a management services organization that anyone can own, linked by a management service agreement. Jackson LLP, Holt Law, and Dike Law Group root it in CPOM; Holt ports it to law firms with three guardrails and a Texas bright line: flat monthly fee or cost plus fair margin passes, percentage of revenue is a no-go. Shikhman puts initial monthly figures at $500 to $1,500. Frederick Shelton turned down about 90% of 70-plus PE-backed MSOs and benchmarks offers against 6 to 8x market multiples. Arizona's ABS track lets non-lawyers own 100% under a compliance lawyer and 10% disclosure. Practitioners split on approval speed, from Rodriguez's March-to-August run and three-minute hearing to 6 to 8 month queues, and on whether PE control of intake captures the firm.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every healthcare-side practitioner starts from one root: the corporate practice of medicine. Erin Jackson of Jackson LLP frames it bluntly: in CPOM or fee-splitting states a person who is not a physician cannot practice medicine, so unlicensed operators cannot own or run the practice, and the MSO lets them manage while steering clear of clinical work, backed by additional contracts and a medical director [4niOtoceEKc @ 00:00:19]. Holt Law describes the move as dividing a healthcare practice in half and says it all boils down to CPOM, which exists to stop non-doctors from making medical decisions [Oa-6OBD0Gak @ 00:00:55]. Jackson's build is two companies: the medical entity employs the doctors, while the MSO takes janitorial, reception, billing, and non-medical hiring and firing [wUqthLNx6Ro @ 00:01:00]. Doris Dike of Dike Law Group adds the threshold question: first decide whether the business is the practice of medicine, because if it is, the operator needs an MSO plus a physician partner, and most states run some form of CPOM [aZDpDRV6-KA @ 00:01:06]. Everyone lands on the same governing document, the management service agreement, which Jackson calls a really complicated contract that must address Stark, Anti-Kickback, the False Claims Act, fee-splitting, and CPOM.

The second point of consensus is the money rule. Jackson says the MSO gets paid a flat fee, monthly or weekly, not based on revenues from patient care [wUqthLNx6Ro @ 00:02:02]. Holt Law ports the identical rule into law firms, where the model was borrowed from healthcare CPOM: the law firm stays 100% lawyer-owned, the MSO takes investors and runs finance, HR, marketing, and IT as a vendor, and three guardrails hold the line: no non-lawyer ownership, no fee sharing, no UPL or influence over lawyer judgment [DNk78wbKy5s @ 00:01:23]. Fee sharing is the risk Holt flags hardest, citing the Texas State Bar's bright line: any compensation model that's a percentage of a law firm's revenue is a no-go, while a flat monthly fee or cost plus a fair margin is the safe path forward [DNk78wbKy5s @ 00:02:51]. Frederick Shelton of Shelton & Steele describes the same split as a law co and a service co, and calls the whole wave a remake of what healthcare went through about 40 years ago, followed by dentistry and accounting [I4F5OYZQJuU @ 00:08:43]. Across both industries, the MSO earns through a defined management fee, never through a cut of professional revenue.

On the Arizona ABS side, every practitioner agrees that non-lawyer money buys ownership, never control of the practice. Lynda Shely, who sits on the Arizona Supreme Court ABS committee, says non-lawyers may own 100% of a firm but cannot direct the representation or choose which clients the firm takes, and that Arizona ABS firms do not permit non-lawyers to practice law [poe1CAsUc4U @ 00:11:33]. Allen Rodriguez, the non-lawyer majority shareholder of Singular Law Group, runs exactly that firewall: product, client experience, operations, automations, scaling, and capital sit with Rodriguez, while lawyers handle legal services [ajveDNkk7dg @ 00:08:59]. Denton Peterson Dunn states the core principle as attorney independence to avoid ethical violations, naming profit-versus-ethics pressure on attorney judgment as the first risk in its rundown [5NeidO5OU60 @ 00:00:47]. Shely repeats the line across both Heart of Law interviews: an ABS law firm is a law firm, it cannot be a referral service, and an office manager cannot sign clients [OdPOa3osKC0 @ 00:12:01]. Shely frames the whole program as voluntary: this is being done for you as an option, not to you, and an Arizona lawyer can say 'I have a law firm in Arizona, it's not an ABS, I'm doing just fine.'

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Inside the MSA, Sara Shikhman, a former general counsel of a multi-state med spa, says the MSO itself is as simple as a standard LLC or corporation that anyone can own; it holds the assets, the equipment, and the brand name, and manages the non-clinical side [JadIHn9B3vk @ 00:02:14]. The MSA is more robust than a medical director agreement, covering scope, assets, leases, and distribution of funds, and it details the management fee, which is how the MSO owner captures revenue. The initial monthly figure Shikhman generally sees is $500 to $1,500, and the medical-director fee gets renegotiated as the business picks up [JadIHn9B3vk @ 00:04:28]. Holt Law draws the asset line with a med spa: Botox, filler, clinical salaries, and, in a conservative view, medical equipment stay clinical, while billing, facility management, and administrative staffing go to the MSO; tension starts when owners push lasers into the MSO [Oa-6OBD0Gak @ 00:03:22]. In California, Holt says non-MDs must use an MSO because CPOM requires greater-than-50% physician ownership, and expanding to more locations may take $10,000 to $100,000 in funding that investors can safely route through the MSO [bXO6V29iXPs @ 00:04:43]. Holt also warns MSOs are not needed for every clinic.

On the law side, Shelton supplies the deal math. Shelton has spoken with over 70 PE-backed MSOs and turned down over 60, about 90% [I4F5OYZQJuU @ 00:06:17]. The red flag Shelton listens for: once we control client intake, then we control the firm. The valuation illustration: a firm whose profit climbs from $3M to $4M to $5M might be valued at about $30M, take $20 to $25M up front plus rollover equity, and see a total package that could exceed $50M [I4F5OYZQJuU @ 00:09:17]. Buyers initially wanted PI firms with $8 to $20M of EBITDA; corporate-backed buyers now look at about $1M, and deals sort into platforms versus bolt-ons. Retiring owners can negotiate put rights, for example $20M up front plus $5M guaranteed in three years. Shelton benchmarks offers hard: 4x profit against the 6 to 8x seen in the market, and waiting until January to close to avoid handing 30 to 40% to taxes [I4F5OYZQJuU @ 00:27:11]. Kvesic's Aprio Legal shows the operating payoff: financial sponsor Charles Bank, an HR team, three-way trust reconciliations, and $500M on AI and tech over five years, with Kvesic admitting a 10-lawyer firm couldn't have afforded that AI software [_P68fUIZN48 @ 00:17:03].

Getting an Arizona ABS license is its own workflow. Shely says the application requires disclosing every person or company with a 10% or greater ownership or economic interest, including holding companies, LLCs, and decision-makers such as a fund manager on the board, plus criminal convictions, civil litigation from the last 10 years, agency investigations, and license revocations, along with plans for confidentiality, trust accounting, conflicts, and docketing [poe1CAsUc4U @ 00:18:08]. On Law Leaders, Shely put applications at 100 to 1,000 pages and approval time stretching from about 4 months to 6 to 8 months, while passive investors under 10% who are not decision-makers skip background checks [Tvn12qG9i5s @ 00:12:25]. Rodriguez reports a leaner experience: a roughly 10-page application, a six thousand dollar hurdle up front, public approval sessions around the first Thursday of each month, and approval in three minutes, with the firm filing in March, winning approval in August, and operating by the end of August [ajveDNkk7dg @ 00:26:16]. Once licensed, the compliance lawyer runs a self-audit every six months, renewal now comes every two years after the June 2025 changes, and fees rose so the program is self-sustaining [OdPOa3osKC0 @ 00:23:51].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The first fork is route selection, and the operators split hard. Holt Law frames the ABS as a non-starter for most firms because Arizona and Utah each needed a law change, while an MSO is viable in most US jurisdictions right now, with the law firm kept 100% lawyer-owned and the MSO taking investors as a vendor [DNk78wbKy5s @ 00:03:52]. Andy Kvesic, CEO of Aprio Legal and an early Arizona ABS licensee, draws the line differently: an MSO cannot own a law firm, an ABS can, and private equity drifted to MSOs mainly because ABS applications take six to eight months [_P68fUIZN48 @ 00:08:46]. Kvesic prices the ABS route bluntly: self-compliance audits twice a year, infractions reported to the ABS committee and the state bar, a mandatory compliance lawyer acting as ethics officer, a license that can be pulled, and renewal every two years. Allen Rodriguez, the non-lawyer majority shareholder of Singular Law Group, reports a much lighter experience from the 2021 cohort: a roughly 10-page application, filed in March, approved in August, and voted through in three minutes at a public session [ajveDNkk7dg @ 00:29:38]. Lynda Shely counters with the current reality: applications now run 100 to 1,000 pages, and time to approval has stretched from about four months to six to eight months [Tvn12qG9i5s @ 00:12:25].

Fee mechanics are where the healthcare and legal camps look aligned on paper but diverge in practice. Holt Law calls the Texas State Bar opinion a bright line rule: any compensation model that's a percentage of a law firm's revenue is a no-go, while a flat monthly fee or cost plus a fair margin is the safe path [DNk78wbKy5s @ 00:02:51]. Erin Jackson of Jackson LLP mirrors that on the medical side, structuring the MSA around a flat fee paid monthly or weekly, not based on revenues from patient care, and built to address Stark, the Anti-Kickback Statute, the False Claims Act, state fee-splitting rules and CPOM [wUqthLNx6Ro @ 00:02:02]. Sara Shikhman, a former general counsel of a multi-state med spa, is more candid about the purpose: the management fee is how the MSO owner captures revenue, generally $500 to $1,500 a month initially, with the medical-director fee renegotiated as the business picks up [JadIHn9B3vk @ 00:04:28]. Kvesic attacks the legal-side asymmetry directly: recruiters routinely take a percentage of first-year revenue from law firms, yet an MSO doing comparable vendor work cannot be paid that way [_P68fUIZN48 @ 00:40:33]. The operator read: flat and cost-plus fees are the shared floor, but the camps disagree on whether the percentage ban is principle or inconsistency.

The deepest split is over whether outside capital on the business side corrupts the practice side. Frederick Shelton of Shelton & Steele reports speaking with more than 70 PE-backed MSOs and turning down over 60, about 90%, and the tell is a single sentence from buyers: once we control client intake, then we control the firm [I4F5OYZQJuU @ 00:28:35]. Kvesic treats that fear as overblown, arguing a well-built MSO only consolidates vendors firms already pay, such as Westlaw or LexisNexis, IT, couriers, AI tools like Harvey, and recruiting, and that non-lawyer ownership isn't automatically a trigger for unethical behavior; Kvesic pegs the loudest critics as personal-injury lawyers [_P68fUIZN48 @ 00:13:23]. Lynda Shely, who sits on the Arizona Supreme Court ABS committee, draws the line at control rather than equity: non-lawyers may own 100% of an Arizona ABS but cannot direct representation or choose which clients the firm takes [poe1CAsUc4U @ 00:11:33]. Denton Peterson Dunn flags high-volume, low-cost work as a quality risk inside ABS firms, then undercuts the alarm by noting that this pressure already exists for traditional lawyers and that lower costs could be good for most clients [5NeidO5OU60 @ 00:01:43].
